table.text: This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Princeton University (Protocol 11968), and all participants provided written informed consent.
The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Princeton University (Protocol 15118).
All participants completed an online-administered version of a fear conditioning task (Fig. 1).
table.formatted: All participants completed an online-administered version of a fear conditioning task (Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

table.text: B) Throughout the task, every few trials, participants were asked to rate how likely they think each stimulus would be followed by a scream (expectancy ratings) on a scale from 0-100%.
This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Princeton University (Protocol 11968), and all participants provided written informed consent.
Participants were recruited from Prolific to complete a series of studies including online behavioral tasks and mental health questionnaires in spring 2023.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Preregistration of analyses on the mechanisms of spontaneous recovery
table.research_questions:
We preregister one hypothesis: Selective maintenance of adverse memories best ex-
plains the spontaneous recovery of fear after extinction. We aim to confirm this hy-
pothesis in two ways and will require both tests to be significant to fully support our
hypothesis:
1. Of the computational models with selective maintenance, the one that fits the data
best will explain the data of participants who show differential spontaneous re-
covery (defined below) better than all of our alternative models without selective
maintenance, as per quantitative model comparison (median BIC for comparing
non-nested models and likelihood ratio test for comparing nested models).
(The full set of models to be considered is listed in the statistical analysis plan;
these models formalize a set of alternative mechanisms for differential sponta-
neous recovery based on the literature and our own ideas.)

2. The effect of selective maintenance will be larger in participants who showed
differential spontaneous recovery than in participants who did not show sponta-
neous recovery in the behavioral task. We will calculate the effect of selective
maintenance using a reparamaterization of parameter estimates from the best
model (see below), and test this with a Wilcoxon rank-sum test.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
All participants completed an online-administered aversive learning and extinction task
inspired by fear acquisition and extinction paradigms widely used in human and animal
research. The paradigm consisted of four phases detailed below. On each trial, partic-
ipants saw one of two conditional stimuli (CSs) and had to press the space bar for the
trial’s outcome. The outcome for one stimulus, the CS+, was an aversive but tolerable
auditory scream US that appeared on 50% of trials in two of the phases. All other CS+
trials, and all trials with the second (CS-) stimulus terminated with no outcome. In all
phases, trials with CS+ and CS- were intermixed in a fixed order for all participants.
The task was completely Pavlovian, meaning that participants’ responses did not deter-
mine what outcomes they would receive; key pressing only served to ensure continued
attention to CSs.
Every three trials, on average, participants rated how likely they expected each CS
to be followed by a scream on a slider scale of 0-100%. Participants completed 31
ratings for each CS. One rating was usually completed before and after each phase (for
a description of the phases, see below). In addition, approximately every 8-10 trials,
participants rated how pleasant or unpleasant they found each stimulus.
The acquisition phase consisted of 8 CS+ trials followed by a US, 8 CS+ trials
with no US, and 10 CS- trials (total: 26 trials). After a 3-5 minute break in which
participants filled out a personality questionnaire, the extinction phase began, which
consisted of 30 trials (18 CS+, 12 CS-, no US). Participants then completed a separate
learning and decision-making task for ∼15 minutes. They then returned to the current
task (note that participants did not know in advance that they would return to the same
task), and completed the third phase, which consisted of a spontaneous recovery test
– 10 trials of the CS+ and 6 trials of the CS- with no US. This phase continued directly
to the last relearning phase, which consisted of 10 presentations of the CS+ (4 of them
reinforced by USs) and 6 presentations of the CS-.
We took a set of measures to ensure that remote participants listened to the aversive
screams throughout the task and experienced them as unpleasant but not intolerable.
Prior to acquisition, participants were instructed to put on headphones. They had to
correctly complete an audio test where they heard a word and had to indicate what
the word was, and the side (left or right) in which they heard it. The goal of the latter
question was to ensure use of headphones. Next, to ensure the scream was not too loud,
participants listened to a clip with the instruction to turn the volume down if they could
hear the speech clearly. This was followed by 6 practice trials with a different CS (a
circle) and a neutral sound US. Finally, participants were presented with an audio clip of the scream and were instructed that they could adjust the volume one last time to
ensure that the scream was unpleasant, but not intolerable.
When starting the second part of the study (the spontaneous recovery test), after
the break in which they completed a different task, participants were first instructed to
rate their expectations of hearing a scream after seeing each image. Subsequently, they
were presented again with the audio clip of the scream and instructed to readjust the
volume to be unpleasant but not intolerable, if needed.
To ensure that participants did not turn down the volume during the task, through-
out the task, participants had to complete six auditory attention checks. During these
attention checks, participants saw a fixation cross and were instructed verbally (in soft
speech that would not be audible had they lowered their volume too much) to press a
specific letter (e.g., the letter ’f’), while they saw the fixation cross.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to any human observation of the data
table.existing_data_explanation:
Data were collected as part of a larger study in which data from over N=755 partici-
pants were collected using several behavioral tasks. The data from this task were split
into two halves. We analyzed the first half (N=378). Here, we are preregistering the
analysis of the second half (N=377). The data were collected online, without
an experimenter observing the data collection process in real time. Since data collec-
tion, nobody (neither us nor any other person) ever observed, quantified or analyzed the data from the second half of the participants.
Hence, we are completely unaware of any patterns or summary statistics from the data,
and they have never been computed.
table.data_collection_procedures:
Participants were recruited from Prolific to complete several online behavioral tasks
and mental health questionnaires in spring 2023. All participants were compensated
for their time (∼ 50 minutes at $13/hr). They had to be at least 18 years old, reside
in the United States, Canada, Australia, or New Zealand, be fluent in English, have
headphones, and have not participated in one of previous similar studies. In general,
participants completed four sessions as part of a larger study. The data to be included
in these analyses were collected as part of the third session, which included the aver-
sive learning task described above and a different learning and decision-making task
between the extinction phase and the spontaneous recovery test, as described above.
Participants were only invited to this session if they passed a variety of attention checks
in the first session.
table.manipulated_variables:
We manipulated the probability of the scream after the CS+ in each phase of the be-
havioral task, so that it was 50% in the acquisition and relearning phase, and 0% in the
extinction and spontaneous recovery test phase.
table.measured_variables:
We measured the participants’ expectation of a scream after each CS several times
during the task. Specifically, participants had to rate on a scale from 0 to 100% for
each CS: ‘How likely do you think each image will be followed by a scream?’ while
viewing images of both CSs.
table.indices:
As the influence of the selective maintenance parameter ω does not only depend on its size,
but also on its size relative to the decay rate γ, we will compute the effect of selective
maintenance SM for each individual based on their parameter estimates as
SM = (1 − γ) · ω/ (γ + (1 − γ) · ω)
table.statistical_tests:
Our generative models, model fitting procedure and statistical analyses plan is described in the attached document 'statistical_analysis_plan.pdf'. 

The code implementing all aspects described in the statistical analysis plan has been uploaded to a private git repository (https://github.com/berwiani/preregistered_analyses_mechanisms_spontaneous_recovery) on 03/11/2025 prior to this preregistration and before the data were accessed. We will make this code available for reviewers and researchers upon reasonable request. We may also make the code publicly available, but given a rapidly changing world with regard to technological developments and the interpretation and application of laws around licenses, we are currently actively evaluating the best pathway for code sharing. 67d1b5b04c909da64944b6e7 statistical_analysis_plan.pdf https://osf.io/project/ucznf/files/osfstorage/67d1b5b04c909da64944b6e7 https://osf.io/download/67d1b5b04c909da64944b6e7 b5ef13d6f96e6cb226875b5a66c1bb0c8757dd94a8ce9fba1860a7fe8512baf6
table.transformations:
Two sets of expectation ratings followed previous sets of ratings without new trials
or relevant time passage (these ratings were before and after instructions and volume
setting). Hence, we will exclude these ratings from the analyses, which will leave us
with 29 ratings per CS per participant.
table.inference_criteria:
We are only preregistering one hypothesis and require all tests we preregister to be
significant to confirm this hypothesis. Thus, we will use α < 0.05 as inference criterion.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
We will exclude participants with incomplete datasets and/or who fail more than two
audio attention checks from all analyses.
Moreover, tests of our key hypothesis will include only subgroups of partic-
ipants defined as follows. First, we will assign participants to subgroups based on
their task behavior: participants who show similar expectations for the CS+ and CS-
at the end of acquisition (< 10 points difference on a scale from 0 to 100%) will be assigned to the ‘Generalizers’ group. The remaining participants will then be divided
into groups based on their behavior on the spontaneous recovery test.1 Participants
who increase their US expectation for the CS+ by more than 10 points compared to
the end of extinction but do not increase their US expectation for the CS- by more than
10 points will be assigned to the ‘spontaneous recovery’ (‘SR’) group – a group that
includes participants who show differential spontaneous recovery, i.e., an increase in
the CS+ rating without a substantial increase in their CS- rating in the spontaneous
recovery test. Participants whose expectations for both stimuli increase by at most 10
points will be assigned to the ‘No SR’ group, and participants whose expectations in-
crease by more than 10 points for both stimuli will be assigned to the ‘Return to Start’
group. Participants who do not meet any of these criteria will not be included in the
subgroup analyses. Note that we use a change in expectation of 10 points as a cutoff
for distinguishing between no SR and SR to account for random response noise.
The criteria of the subgroups were inspired by two aspects: 1) In pilot data (not
part of this analysis), we qualitatively observed that most participants fall into one of
these subgroups. 2) Our goal is to explain specific behavioral patterns, particularly,
differential spontaneous recovery. These subgroups allow us to focus our analyses and
hypothesis on mechanisms of spontaneous recovery of predictions for the CS+ (as in
the ‘SR’ versus ‘no SR’ groups) while leaving aside (for now) other mechanisms that
pertain to both stimuli together (as seen in the ‘Generalizers’ and ‘Return to Start’
groups) as more power would be needed to provide robust evidence for these other
mechanisms that we so far only observed in smaller subgroups.
table.missing_data_handling:
Participants with missing data will be excluded. As reliable and comparable parameter
estimates can only be achieved when people completed the whole task, non-completers
will be excluded. Since participants can only proceed with the task after a response,
missing data during the task are assumed to be rare and can only occur due to technical
failure.
table.exploratory_analyses:
On an exploratory level, we will compare differences in parameter estimates of the
winning model between the ‘Return to Start’ and ‘Generalizers’ group and the other
two subgroups.
We also expect, based on our previous results, that the best model with selective
maintenance will best explain the behavior of the whole sample. We will test for this,
but as this result depends on the number of people showing spontaneous recovery, we
preregister this hypothesis only for the SR group, as above.

plains the spontaneous recovery of fear after extinction. We aim to confirm this hy-
pothesis in two ways and will require both tests to be significant to fully support our
hypothesis:
1. Of the computational models with selective maintenance, the one that fits the data
best will explain the data of participants who show differential spontaneous re-
covery (defined below) better than all of our alternative models without selective
maintenance, as per quantitative model comparison (median BIC for comparing
non-nested models and likelihood ratio test for comparing nested models).
(The full set of models to be considered is listed in the statistical analysis plan;
these models formalize a set of alternative mechanisms for differential sponta-
neous recovery based on the literature and our own ideas.)

2. The effect of selective maintenance will be larger in participants who showed
differential spontaneous recovery than in participants who did not show sponta-
neous recovery in the behavioral task. We will calculate the effect of selective
maintenance using a reparamaterization of parameter estimates from the best
model (see below), and test this with a Wilcoxon rank-sum test.", "Other", "No blinding is involved in this study.", "All participants completed an online-administered aversive learning and extinction task
inspired by fear acquisition and extinction paradigms widely used in human and animal
research. The paradigm consisted of four phases detailed below. On each trial, partic-
ipants saw one of two conditional stimuli (CSs) and had to press the space bar for the
trial’s outcome. The outcome for one stimulus, the CS+, was an aversive but tolerable
auditory scream US that appeared on 50% of trials in two of the phases. All other CS+
trials, and all trials with the second (CS-) stimulus terminated with no outcome. In all
phases, trials with CS+ and CS- were intermixed in a fixed order for all participants.
The task was completely Pavlovian, meaning that participants’ responses did not deter-
mine what outcomes they would receive; key pressing only served to ensure continued
attention to CSs.
Every three trials, on average, participants rated how likely they expected each CS
to be followed by a scream on a slider scale of 0-100%. Participants completed 31
ratings for each CS. One rating was usually completed before and after each phase (for
a description of the phases, see below). In addition, approximately every 8-10 trials,
participants rated how pleasant or unpleasant they found each stimulus.
The acquisition phase consisted of 8 CS+ trials followed by a US, 8 CS+ trials
with no US, and 10 CS- trials (total: 26 trials). After a 3-5 minute break in which
participants filled out a personality questionnaire, the extinction phase began, which
consisted of 30 trials (18 CS+, 12 CS-, no US). Participants then completed a separate
learning and decision-making task for ∼15 minutes. They then returned to the current
task (note that participants did not know in advance that they would return to the same
task), and completed the third phase, which consisted of a spontaneous recovery test
– 10 trials of the CS+ and 6 trials of the CS- with no US. This phase continued directly
to the last relearning phase, which consisted of 10 presentations of the CS+ (4 of them
reinforced by USs) and 6 presentations of the CS-.
We took a set of measures to ensure that remote participants listened to the aversive
screams throughout the task and experienced them as unpleasant but not intolerable.
Prior to acquisition, participants were instructed to put on headphones. They had to
correctly complete an audio test where they heard a word and had to indicate what
the word was, and the side (left or right) in which they heard it. The goal of the latter
question was to ensure use of headphones. Next, to ensure the scream was not too loud,
participants listened to a clip with the instruction to turn the volume down if they could
hear the speech clearly. This was followed by 6 practice trials with a different CS (a
circle) and a neutral sound US. Finally, participants were presented with an audio clip of the scream and were instructed that they could adjust the volume one last time to
ensure that the scream was unpleasant, but not intolerable.
When starting the second part of the study (the spontaneous recovery test), after
the break in which they completed a different task, participants were first instructed to
rate their expectations of hearing a scream after seeing each image. Subsequently, they
were presented again with the audio clip of the scream and instructed to readjust the
volume to be unpleasant but not intolerable, if needed.
To ensure that participants did not turn down the volume during the task, through-
out the task, participants had to complete six auditory attention checks. During these
attention checks, participants saw a fixation cross and were instructed verbally (in soft
speech that would not be audible had they lowered their volume too much) to press a
specific letter (e.g., the letter ’f’), while they saw the fixation cross.", "Registration prior to any human observation of the data", "Data were collected as part of a larger study in which data from over N=755 partici-
pants were collected using several behavioral tasks. The data from this task were split
into two halves. We analyzed the first half (N=378). Here, we are preregistering the
analysis of the second half (N=377). The data were collected online, without
an experimenter observing the data collection process in real time. Since data collec-
tion, nobody (neither us nor any other person) ever observed, quantified or analyzed the data from the second half of the participants.
Hence, we are completely unaware of any patterns or summary statistics from the data,
and they have never been computed.", "Participants were recruited from Prolific to complete several online behavioral tasks
and mental health questionnaires in spring 2023. All participants were compensated

participants completed four sessions as part of a larger study. The data to be included

sive learning task described above and a different learning and decision-making task
between the extinction phase and the spontaneous recovery test, as described above.
Participants were only invited to this session if they passed a variety of attention checks

Moreover, tests of our key hypothesis will include only subgroups of partic-
ipants defined as follows. First, we will assign participants to subgroups based on
their task behavior: participants who show similar expectations for the CS+ and CS-
at the end of acquisition (< 10 points difference on a scale from 0 to 100%) will be assigned to the ‘Generalizers’ group. The remaining participants will then be divided
into groups based on their behavior on the spontaneous recovery test.1 Participants
who increase their US expectation for the CS+ by more than 10 points compared to
the end of extinction but do not increase their US expectation for the CS- by more than

includes participants who show differential spontaneous recovery, i.e., an increase in

crease by more than 10 points for both stimuli will be assigned to the ‘Return to Start’
group. Participants who do not meet any of these criteria will not be included in the
subgroup analyses. Note that we use a change in expectation of 10 points as a cutoff
for distinguishing between no SR and SR to account for random response noise.
The criteria of the subgroups were inspired by two aspects: 1) In pilot data (not
part of this analysis), we qualitatively observed that most participants fall into one of

groups) as more power would be needed to provide robust evidence for these other

table.formatted: Wilcoxon rank-sum tests showed that the SR group had marginally higher expectations of negative outcomes for CS+ in acquisition (Z = 1.96, p = .05, r = .12; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">3A</ref>), a larger increase in expectations of negative outcomes for the CS+ after the first break between acquisition and extinction (Z = 2.03, p = .04, r = .13; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">3B</ref>), a larger decrease in expectation of negative outcomes for the CS+ during extinction (Z = 4.93, p < .001, r = .30, Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">3C</ref>); higher differential SR (see below) in the spontaneous recovery test (as expected given that this measure closely related to our categorization criterion; Z = 13.16, p < .001, r = .81; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">3D</ref>); and stronger increase of that expectation in the relearning phase (Z = 4.03, p < .001, r = .25; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">3E</ref>).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p > .28", "p > .16", "p > .24", 
"p > .35", "p < .02", "p > .23"), Text = c("Note, however, that the two groups showed no difference in negative outcome expectations before starting the task for each of CS+ alone, CSalone or the difference between them (all p > .28).", 
"There were no differences in the simulated predictions of outcomes for each of the CSs in the first trial of the task, before observing any outcomes (p > .16 for all comparisons).", 
"Importantly, no model without selective maintenance captured the significant differences in differential spontaneous recovery between the two groups (p > .24 for all comparisons).", 
"Wilcoxon rank-sum tests did not indicate differences between the groups on any of these measures (p > .35 for all comparisons).", 
"Additional exploratory analyses also replicated our previous results, showing that the Return to Start group (median (IQR): 0.73 (0.55-0.81)) showed more decay than the SR (median (IQR): 0.91 (0.88-0.94)) and No SR groups (median (IQR): 0.94 (0.90-0.98); Z = -7.71, p < .001, r = .51, and Z = -8.54, p < .001, r = .66, respectively; Fig. 6E) and that participants in the Generalizers group were best fit with a more stochastic prior (i.e., a greater prior parameter; median (IQR): 0.80 (0.07-2.25)) than participants in all other groups (SR group: median (IQR): 2.34 × 10 -7 (5 × 10 -10 -4.42 × 10 -6 )); Z = 4.15, p < .001, r = .31, No SR group: median (IQR): 3.22 × 10 -7 (0 -1 × 10 -5 )); Z = 3.96, p < .001, r = .36, Return to Start group: median (IQR): 2.13 × 10 -4 (0 -0.2408); Z = 2.43, p < .02, r = .30; Fig. 6H).", 
"Again, there were no differences in affective ratings between the two groups for the CS+ or the CSstimulus alone or for their difference before the first trial (all p > .23)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. live_data_statements: All participants completed an online-administered version of a fear conditioning task (Fig. 1).
B) Throughout the task, every few trials, participants were asked to rate how likely they think each stimulus would be followed by a scream (expectancy ratings) on a scale from 0-100%.
This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Princeton University (Protocol 11968), and all participants provided written informed consent.
Participants were recruited from Prolific to complete a series of studies including online behavioral tasks and mental health questionnaires in spring 2023.
All participants were compensated for their time at a rate of $13/hr.
To qualify for the study, participants had to reside in the United States, Canada, Australia, or New Zealand, be fluent in English, and have headphones.
From the exploration dataset, 23 participants were excluded due to incomplete datasets and 37 participants were excluded due to failing more than two audio attention checks.
An event listener was then activated and the participant had 6000 ms to press the space bar before the trial timed out.
Every three trials, on average, participants were asked to rate how likely they expected each of the two CSs would be followed by a scream on a scale of 0-100% using two horizontal slider bars.
Participants completed 31 ratings for each CS.

This phase was followed by a 3-5 minute break in which participants completed a filler questionnaire of no interest (the 20-item short form International Personality Item Pool-Five-Factor Model measure; Donnellan, Oswald, Baird, & Lucas, 2006).

Next, participants completed a separate task (a risky decision making task in which they made choices between a sure 5-point reward and a stimulus with an unknown but learnable chance of giving 10 points or 0 points; not analyzed here) for ∼15 minutes.

As participants were tested online and from remotely, to ensure they heard the US loudly enough and did not reduce the volume throughout the task, participants completed a set of volume calibration steps and six auditory attention checks were spread throughout the task (see Suppl.

In two separate online sessions, participants completed the GAD7 questionnaire (prior to completing the task; Spitzer, Kroenke, Williams, and Löwe (2006); Löwe et al. (2008)), several subscales of the HiTOP questionnaire (several weeks after completing the task; Watson, Forbes, et al. (2022)), as well as other symptom self-report questionnaires not analyzed here.
Participants were invited to complete the HiTOP questions up to several weeks after completing the task.
However, we note that participants were instructed to indicate for each statement "Have there been significant times during the last 12 months in which the following statements applied to you?"

The remaining participants were then categorized into groups based on their behavior on the spontaneous recovery test, in particular, their first rating of expectation of a scream for both the CS+ and the CS-, which occurred immediately at the beginning of the spontaneous recovery test phase before any other exposure to the stimuli or screams or audio instructions.

Participants and procedure Participants were recruited to take part in an online study of a self-help tool for symptoms of depression/low mood and lack of energy.

text.text: Return of fear after exposure poses a significant challenge for treatment of anxiety disorders.
In this study, we used computational modeling to test competing mechanisms underlying spontaneous recovery of fear over time.

We fit computational models of a novel theory of spontaneous recovery-selective maintenance of aversive memoriesto behavior from a fear conditioning and extinction task (N=316), and showed that they uniquely captured spontaneous recovery and quantitatively outperformed alternative models embodying theories from the literature.
The results were supported across multiple datasets, including a preregistered replication (N=355) and a sample with internalizing symptoms (N=520).
The selective maintenance modeling framework additionally offers mechanistic insights into overgeneralization and the development of anxiety.
Indeed, in the sample with internalizing symptoms we found that symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder correlated with estimates of overgeneralization in the model.
Through simulations, we further demonstrated that insights from our model can explain how targeted interventions such as retrieval cues and cognitive interventions can prevent the return of fear.
These results highlight selective maintenance of aversive events in memory as a critical and testable target for improving anxiety treatments and preventing relapse.
Exposure-based interventions are among the most effective treatments for many anxieties (Ougrin, 2011).
text.formatted: Exposure-based interventions are among the most effective treatments for many anxieties <ref type="bibr">(Ougrin, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: During exposure, an individual confronts a feared stimulus or situation without experiencing the expected negative outcome.
A common assumption is that learning from this experience leads to decreased prediction of the negative outcome, and thus a reduction of fear.
However, fear often returns after some time, and up to 62% of individuals relapse (Craske & Mystkowski, 2006).
text.formatted: However, fear often returns after some time, and up to 62% of individuals relapse <ref type="bibr">(Craske & Mystkowski, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: To develop clinical methods that prevent relapse, it is critical that we understand why fear returns.
Exposure has been studied extensively with well established fear conditioning and extinction paradigms.

In such paradigms, in the acquisition phase, a neutral stimulus, often called a CS+ (for conditional stimulus), is paired with an aversive stimulus (US; unconditional stimulus), leading to fear responses when confronted with the CS+.
In the subsequent extinction phase, mimicking exposure therapy, the CS+ is presented without the US.
This procedure leads to a reduction in fear of the CS+.
Strikingly, after the passage of time and even without new exposure to the CS+ or US, fear of the CS+ often returns.
This phenomenon of 'spontaneous recovery' is well established across species and seems to be time-dependent (Rescorla, 2004; Quirk, 2002; Robbins, 1990; Haberlandt, Hamsher, & Kennedy, 1978).
text.formatted: This phenomenon of 'spontaneous recovery' is well established across species and seems to be time-dependent <ref type="bibr">(Rescorla, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Quirk, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Robbins, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haberlandt, Hamsher, & Kennedy, 1978)</ref>.

text.text: Fear can only return if the 'fear memory' (i.e., a memory that associates the CS+ and the US) still exists in the brain after the extinction phase.

Indeed, theories of return of fear usually contain the notion that acquisition events and extinction events give rise to separate associations, and thus to separate memories (Bouton, 1993; Gershman, Jones, Norman, Monfils, & Niv, 2013; Craske et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Indeed, theories of return of fear usually contain the notion that acquisition events and extinction events give rise to separate associations, and thus to separate memories <ref type="bibr">(Bouton, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gershman, Jones, Norman, Monfils, & Niv, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Craske et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: These two memories are assumed to compete for retrieval during subsequent presentations of the CS+.
At the end of extinction, the extinction memory is stronger, hence the reduction of apparent fear.
For spontaneous recovery to occur, the strength of the fear memory must increase relative to the strength of the extinction memory.
As such, while separation of the representations of dangerous and safe latent causes (contexts; memories) is a necessary prerequisite for explaining spontaneous recovery, it alone is not sufficient.
We still need to explain the change in relative strengths of the two competing associations.

Inspired by evidence of decay of memory but better memory for emotionally charged events over time (Dalgleish & Hitchcock, 2023; Rouhani, Niv, Frank, & Schwabe, 2023), and neural evidence that reactivation can prevent memory decay processes (Wimmer, Liu, McNamee, & Dolan, 2023), we propose that spontaneous recovery can be explained through a mechanism we term 'selective maintenance' -maintenance of memories that counteracts their decay, and is specific to memories of negative experiences.
text.formatted: Inspired by evidence of decay of memory but better memory for emotionally charged events over time <ref type="bibr">(Dalgleish & Hitchcock, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Rouhani, Niv, Frank, & Schwabe, 2023)</ref>, and neural evidence that reactivation can prevent memory decay processes <ref type="bibr">(Wimmer, Liu, McNamee, & Dolan, 2023)</ref>, we propose that spontaneous recovery can be explained through a mechanism we term 'selective maintenance' -maintenance of memories that counteracts their decay, and is specific to memories of negative experiences.

text.text: According to the selective maintenance idea, as memories of dangerous and safe experiences decay over time, dangerous memories are spared some of this decay, perhaps because they are reactivated periodically or due to other processes that are selective to dangerous memories.

This slower decay rate of dangerous but not safe memories changes the balance such that over time, the acquisition memory becomes relatively stronger compared to the extinction memory, explaining why responses to the CS+ change accordingly.

Here, we aim to investigate whether selective maintenance can explain the detailed pattern of and individual differences in spontaneous recovery, and whether it can do so better than a set of alternative theories from the literature (see Rescorla (2004) for a review of the key theories, which we will model).
text.formatted: Here, we aim to investigate whether selective maintenance can explain the detailed pattern of and individual differences in spontaneous recovery, and whether it can do so better than a set of alternative theories from the literature (see <ref type="bibr">Rescorla (2004)</ref> for a review of the key theories, which we will model).

text.text: Specifically, we will contrast selective maintenance with recency weighting (Devenport, 1998), neural processing fatigue (Pavlov, 1927), and increased salience of aversive events (see Suppl.
text.formatted: Specifically, we will contrast selective maintenance with recency weighting <ref type="bibr">(Devenport, 1998)</ref>, neural processing fatigue <ref type="bibr">(Pavlov, 1927)</ref>, and increased salience of aversive events (see Suppl.

text.text: Subsec.
2.3 for a discussion of other alternative mechanisms).

To compare these theories quantitatively and qualitatively, we first formulate the selective maintenance hypothesis as a computational model using the latent cause framework (Gershman, Blei, & Niv, 2010).
text.formatted: To compare these theories quantitatively and qualitatively, we first formulate the selective maintenance hypothesis as a computational model using the latent cause framework <ref type="bibr">(Gershman, Blei, & Niv, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: We use this same latent-cause framework to model reduced variants without selective maintenance, as well as the alternative theories from the literature introduced above.
We fit each model to empirical data that we collected from individual participants who completed a fear conditioning and extinction paradigm.

We then compare the models quantitatively in terms of how well they predict the empirical data, and qualitatively in terms of their ability to generate spontaneous recovery after extinction as well as all other features of the behavioral data.
In our exploration dataset, we show that models incorporating selective maintenance provide the best quantitative and qualitative fit to the data.
We replicate this pattern of results in preregistered analyses of an unseen dataset from the same study, as well as in data from a separate study with individuals with internalizing symptoms.

Based on these modeling results, we therefore hypothesize that selective maintenance may be related to the emergence and maintenance of specific anxiety-related symptoms after aversive events, while a tendency to group disparate events in a single latent cause (i.e., overgeneralization) may be associated with symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder.
We therefore test for associations between model parameters and anxiety symptoms in both our our sample from the general population and our sample with internalizing symptoms.

Finally, we use the insights gained from our model to propose modifications to exposure therapy that target mechanisms driving spontaneous recovery so as to prevent the return of fear and illustrate the potential effects of such interventions through simulations.

Subsequently, we report replications of the main results in a second dataset (preregistered analyses on a replication dataset from Study 1) and a dataset from a study with individuals with symptoms of depression (Study 2).

text.text: A) The task consisted of 4 phases.
On each trial, participants observed an image of a moon (CS+) or candles (CS-).
First, in the acquisition phase, the CS+ was followed by a loud aversive auditory scream (US) on 8 of 16 trials.
The CS-was never followed by a US.
After a short break (completing a questionnaire for 3-5 minutes), in the extinction phase, no stimulus was followed by the US.
After a longer break (completing a different task for 15-20 minutes), a spontaneous recovery (SR) test phase was conducted without any USs.
Immediately afterwards, a relearning phase began, in which the CS+ was followed by the US on 4 of 10 trials.
B) Throughout the task, every few trials, participants were asked to rate how likely they think each stimulus would be followed by a scream (expectancy ratings) on a scale from 0-100%.
Occasionally, they were also asked to indicate their emotional response to each stimulus (affective ratings).

text.text: Visual inspection of a pilot study (not part of this dataset) suggested that participants' behavior fell into four different subgroups.
Simulations with computational models further suggested that the behavior of each subgroup might arise from different mechanisms.

To be able to test these mechanistic hypotheses quantitatively, we used the pilot data and simulations to devise a set of criteria to divide participants into four subgroups based on their behavioral response profile (see Data Categorization in Methods).

We applied these criteria to our exploratory dataset after the data were collected, to categorize participants into the following subgroups: a spontaneous recovery ('SR') group (participants who showed an increase in CS+ but not CS-expectancy ratings in the spontaneous recovery test; Fig. 2B); a 'No SR' group (participants who did not show an increase in expectation of the scream in the spontaneous recovery test; Fig. 2C); a 'Return to Start' group (participants who showed an increase in expectations of screams for both CS+ and CS-in the spontaneous recovery test; Fig. 2D); and a 'Generalizers' group (participants who did not differentiate between the CS+ and the CS-at the end of acquisition; Fig. 2E).
text.formatted: We applied these criteria to our exploratory dataset after the data were collected, to categorize participants into the following subgroups: a spontaneous recovery ('SR') group (participants who showed an increase in CS+ but not CS-expectancy ratings in the spontaneous recovery test; Fig. <ref type="figure">2B</ref>); a 'No SR' group (participants who did not show an increase in expectation of the scream in the spontaneous recovery test; Fig. <ref type="figure">2C</ref>); a 'Return to Start' group (participants who showed an increase in expectations of screams for both CS+ and CS-in the spontaneous recovery test; Fig. <ref type="figure">2D</ref>); and a 'Generalizers' group (participants who did not differentiate between the CS+ and the CS-at the end of acquisition; Fig. <ref type="figure">2E</ref>).

text.text: Note that the Generalizers group showed signs of extinction and differentiated CS+ and CS-in the relearning phase, suggesting they were not simply inattentive.
Most participants (all but N=53) fell into the SR (N=175) and No SR (N=88) groups.
To examine the mechanisms of spontaneous recovery, we therefore focused our analyses mostly on these two groups.
First, we compared the behavior of the SR and No SR groups by analyzing responses for the CS+ (compared to those for the CS-) in the different task phases.

Wilcoxon rank-sum tests showed that the SR group had marginally higher expectations of negative outcomes for CS+ in acquisition (Z = 1.96, p = .05, r = .12; Fig. 3A), a larger increase in expectations of negative outcomes for the CS+ after the first break between acquisition and extinction (Z = 2.03, p = .04, r = .13; Fig. 3B), a larger decrease in expectation of negative outcomes for the CS+ during extinction (Z = 4.93, p < .001, r = .30, Fig. 3C); higher differential SR (see below) in the spontaneous recovery test (as expected given that this measure closely related to our categorization criterion; Z = 13.16, p < .001, r = .81; Fig. 3D); and stronger increase of that expectation in the relearning phase (Z = 4.03, p < .001, r = .25; Fig. 3E).

text.text: Thus, the two groups differed significantly during all phases of the task, and not only in the spontaneous recovery test.
Note, however, that the two groups showed no difference in negative outcome expectations before starting the task for each of CS+ alone, CSalone or the difference between them (all p > .28).

Tab 2.
Our main aim was to uncover why fear returns with time.

To ensure that our behavioral measure of the amount of return of fear was not confounded by processes such as less effective extinction, regression to the mean, or overall decay of memories, we used a measure of "differential SR" throughout our analyses.

We computed differential SR as the expectancy rating for the CS+ at the beginning of the spontaneous recovery test (rating at the start of the phase, after the break and before seeing any trials) minus the last expectancy rating for the CS+ in extinction, minus the same metric for the CS-.
Differential SR therefore measures the specific change in expectations of a scream for the CS+ during the break, above and beyond any change in expectations for the CS-.
We observed a similar pattern of results when we analyzed the affective ratings using the same approach as for the expectancy ratings (see Suppl.
Subsec.
2.2 for details).
Given the correspondence between the two measures, and because we had more ratings of expectancies, we focused on the latter for all subsequent computational modeling analyses.

To understand why spontaneous recovery might arise, we formulated different mechanistic theories (or hypotheses) as computational models and compared them quantitatively (in terms of fit to the empirical data) and qualitatively (in terms of their ability to generate spontaneous recovery).

We note that a central challenge for participants-both in our task and in daily life-is that they do not know the true structure of the environment (e.g., the designation of phases and their boundaries in the task).
Instead, they must infer this structure based on past experiences, in order to make accurate predictions.

text.text: our models.

Here, we first describe the building blocks of this framework, and then outline the additional components we included in each model that we fitted to our data (increasing the complexity and adding alternative mechanisms as we proceed).
For detailed descriptions and formalizations of each model, see Subsec.
'Generative Models' in the Methods section.
In latent cause inference (Gershman et al., 2010), on each trial the participant infers whether the current observation results from an old (previously inferred) latent cause or a new latent cause.
text.formatted: In latent cause inference <ref type="bibr">(Gershman et al., 2010)</ref>, on each trial the participant infers whether the current observation results from an old (previously inferred) latent cause or a new latent cause.

text.text: This inference, which is probabilistic (i.e., due to uncertainty about the structure of the task, a trial can be assigned in part to several latent causes), is influenced by at least three factors: 1) the strength of old latent causes, formalized as counts N of how many trials (or fractions of trials) had been inferred to come from each latent cause in the past (the stronger the latent cause, the more likely it will be inferred again), 2) the a priori probability of a new latent cause, formalized through a "concentration parameter" α (the larger α the more likely is a new latent cause), and 3) the participant's belief about the variability of observations that each latent cause generates, formalized here (for binary observations) as a beta function with one free parameter a obs .

The smaller a obs , the more deterministic (0 or 1) are the probabilities associating the latent cause with each observation, and therefore a new latent cause is more likely to be inferred if a previously observed stimulus is omitted, or vice versa (see Fig. 4A-D for an example).
text.formatted: The smaller a obs , the more deterministic (0 or 1) are the probabilities associating the latent cause with each observation, and therefore a new latent cause is more likely to be inferred if a previously observed stimulus is omitted, or vice versa (see Fig. <ref type="figure">4A-D</ref> for an example).

text.text: Inference in this basic latent cause model is not sensitive to time or order of events (Aldous, Ibragimov, Jacod, & Aldous, 1985), and therefore the model cannot account for time-dependent phenomena such as spontaneous recovery.
text.formatted: Inference in this basic latent cause model is not sensitive to time or order of events <ref type="bibr">(Aldous, Ibragimov, Jacod, & Aldous, 1985)</ref>, and therefore the model cannot account for time-dependent phenomena such as spontaneous recovery.

text.text: To capture the notion that past events are less relevant for present inferences, we decayed the counts of past events by γ ∈ [0, 1] on each trial (Blei & Frazier, 2011).
text.formatted: To capture the notion that past events are less relevant for present inferences, we decayed the counts of past events by γ ∈ [0, 1] on each trial <ref type="bibr">(Blei & Frazier, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: However, simulations show that this decay is not sufficient to explain spontaneous recovery of fear over time, as it does not change the relative strength of different latent causes over time.
To address this, we modeled relative strengthening over time of latent causes that predict the US, perhaps because they are reactivated in memory.

We termed this mechanism "selective maintenance" and formalized it as an increase of the decay parameter γ (leading to less decay) by a selective maintenance parameter ω in proportion to the probability that the latent cause is assumed to lead to an aversive US (Fig. 4E).
text.formatted: We termed this mechanism "selective maintenance" and formalized it as an increase of the decay parameter γ (leading to less decay) by a selective maintenance parameter ω in proportion to the probability that the latent cause is assumed to lead to an aversive US (Fig. <ref type="figure">4E</ref>).

text.text: To summarize, in our selective maintenance models, all latent causes decay, however, latent causes associated with aversive outcomes decay less due to the effect of selective maintenance.
This leads over time to a relative strengthening of aversive latent causes as compared to other causes.

Finally, to allow for individual differences in selective maintenance (i.e., some participants may reactivate memories throughout the task while others may do so only during the break), we introduced C low , a low-salience parameter that decreases the counts of events with aversive outcomes when they occur (e.g., during acquisition).
During the task, low salience of US events effectively counteracts selective maintenance (which increases the relative strength of latent causes associated with aversive outcomes).
However, low salience has no effect during the break, when the effect of selective maintenance can fully unfold.
Note that this mechanism was not crucial for explaining spontaneous recovery, but it allowed our model to better capture behavior from a larger variety of individuals.
Thus, our final model had four free parameters: prior a obs , decay γ, selective maintenance ω, and low salience C low .
We quantitatively compared this model to four reduced versions of itself to test whether each component of the model is necessary.
We also evaluated several models that formalized alternative theoretical accounts of spontaneous recovery from the literature.

These included a "Salience Model" that used a salience parameter C for the count for each trial with a US (i.e., in this model a trial with a scream US counts as C trials), to capture the notion that aversive events might be more strongly encoded.

We modeled Devenport's (1998) proposal that spontaneous recovery might arise over time due to recency weighting of events in a "Temporal Weighting Model" with a power-law decay of latent-cause counts.
text.formatted: We modeled <ref type="bibr">Devenport's (1998)</ref> proposal that spontaneous recovery might arise over time due to recency weighting of events in a "Temporal Weighting Model" with a power-law decay of latent-cause counts.

text.text: Finally, we formalized Pavlov's (1927) suggestion that repeated stimulus presentations reduce processing over time and thus lead to less learning during extinction in a "Processing Loss Model" where the count of each trial was reduced according to the number of times its CS had already been observed.
text.formatted: Finally, we formalized <ref type="bibr">Pavlov's (1927)</ref> suggestion that repeated stimulus presentations reduce processing over time and thus lead to less learning during extinction in a "Processing Loss Model" where the count of each trial was reduced according to the number of times its CS had already been observed.

text.text: Each of these three alternative models had free parameters governing the processes of interest (see Methods).
Overall, this led to eight models, which we also compared to a "Basic α Model" with vanilla latent cause inference and only the concentration parameter as a free parameter.
The winning model was reliably recoverable from simulated data when compared to non-nested alternative models (see Suppl.
Subsec.

We compared the different models by fitting each model to the trial-by-trial data of each participant and calculating Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) scores from the likelihood of the data with the best fit parameters, penalized for the number of free parameters.
We next computed the difference of the AIC values of the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model and all other models for each participant.
Negative values indicated that the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model explained the data better in these comparisons.

text.text: We focused the remaining analyses of the exploratory dataset on the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model given that it captured the data best (the Selective Maintenance Model showed a similar pattern of results).
We formalized three independent hypotheses based on simulations of the Selective Maintenance Model.

First, participants who show spontaneous recovery (SR group) should have more selective maintenance of aversive events (as this is what leads to the relative strengthening of the dangerous latent cause during breaks, and therefore to spontaneous recovery of the prediction of the scream).

Second, participants whose predictions of screams return to start-of-experiment levels after the long break (Return to Start group) should show a higher rate of decay of events in memory (as this promotes the creation of new latent causes after the break, with their initial prediction levels).

Third, participants who fail to distinguish between the CS+ and CS-stimuli during acquisition (Generalizers group) should have more stochastic priors (thus they tend to infer a single latent cause that accounts for observations of both types of stimuli).
Due to smaller sample sizes in the Return to Start and Generalizers group, we were not necessarily powered to test the second and third hypotheses and treated these analyses as exploratory.
All parameters of the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model were reliably recoverable (r = .75 -.99, see Suppl.
Subsec.
2.6), and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests supported all three hypotheses.

First, estimates of the selective maintenance parameter ω were higher in the SR group than in the No SR group (median (IQR): SR group = 0.49 (0.23-0.73), No SR group = 0.28 (0.01-0.72); Z = 3.19, p = .001, r = .20).

This was even more evident when reparameterizing ω ′ = (1-γ)•ω (1-γ)•ω+γ , which quantifies the proportion of memory of counts due to selective maintenance, which we call 'effective selective maintenance' (median (IQR): SR group = 0.04 (0.02-0.06), No SR group = 0.01 (0.00-0.03); Z = 5.32, p < .001, r = .33, Fig. 6A).

text.text: Spontaneous recovery was driven by the return of the dangerous latent cause.

We hypothesized that spontaneous recovery occurs because the strength of the dangerous latent cause becomes higher increases relative to that of the safe latent cause associated with the CS+ during the break before the spontaneous recovery test.

To examine this, we computed the change in relative strength of each of the two latent causes between the end of extinction and the beginning of the spontaneous recovery test and computed the difference in that change between the two latent causes (dangerous latent cause minus safe CS+ latent cause).

In line with the assumption that this effect is driven by selective maintenance, effective selective maintenance estimates (ω ′ ) correlated with the difference in change in strength between the two latent causes across participants in the SR and No SR groups (ρ = .76, p < .001; Fig. 9A).

text.text: Furthermore, in line with the assumption that these latent cause changes drive spontaneous recovery, this metric of latent cause change also correlated with empirical differential spontaneous recovery (ρ = .49, p < .001; Fig. 9B).

text.text: Anxiety disorders are highly prevalent.
While effective treatments such as exposure therapy exist, symptoms often return even after successful therapy, and anxiety relapses (Craske, Hermans, & Vansteenwegen, 2006).
text.formatted: While effective treatments such as exposure therapy exist, symptoms often return even after successful therapy, and anxiety relapses <ref type="bibr">(Craske, Hermans, & Vansteenwegen, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Our model can, at least in principle, explain why and when different anxiety disorders will develop and return.

If the mechanisms quantified by our model are causally involved in the development, maintenance, and return of anxiety symptoms, and assuming we can measure these mechanisms with sufficient precision through our task and model parameters, these parameters should be able to predict the course of anxiety in individuals.
A randomized controlled study design is needed to fully test such hypotheses.
Here, as a first pass, we examined whether these mechanisms are associated with self-reported symptoms of anxiety.

Our exploratory analysis was guided by two hypotheses: first, stochastic priors over observations (high a obs ) can lead to a spread of fear to many stimuli, and therefore this parameter may be associated with symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD).
Since we had self-reported GAD symptoms in all our datasets, for these analyses we included all participants from each dataset.

Second, selective maintenance of aversive events might strengthen the memory or imagination of aversive events and thus drive the development and maintenance of specific anxiety disorders (such as phobias).

As selective maintenance could only be reliably estimated in the SR and No SR groups, we only included these subgroups when examining the association between the effective amount of selective maintenance and symptoms of specific anxiety disorders.
In these analyses, we took a dimensional approach and examined associations of symptoms of different anxiety disorders with model parameters regardless of formal diagnosis status of a participant.

This is in line with the HiTOP consortium's recommendations to adopt a dimensional conceptualization of psychopathology (Kotov et al., 2021) and with the view that crossing the threshold to receive an anxiety disorder diagnosis does not result from or imply different underlying mechanisms from those causing subthreshold symptoms (e.g., Haslam (2003)).

text.text: Considering that extinction and spontaneous recovery are models of exposure therapy and relapse in anxiety disorders, we propose that the mechanistic insight gained from modeling such behavior can be used to improve interventions of exposure therapy.

Specifically, the model suggests that intervening in any of its building blocksdeterministic priors, memory decay, or selective maintenance of aversive memoriescould help prevent spontaneous recovery.
Two interventions proposed in the literature have already been empirically shown to reduce the amount of return of fear.

These are: spreading extinction trials (exposure sessions) over longer time intervals (Laborda, McConnell, & Miller, 2011) or tagging the 'safe' (exposure) memory with a retrieval cue such as a wristband that clients can then wear and use as cue to recall that memory (Craske, Treanor, Conway, Zbozinek, & Vervliet, 2014).
text.formatted: These are: spreading extinction trials (exposure sessions) over longer time intervals <ref type="bibr">(Laborda, McConnell, & Miller, 2011)</ref> or tagging the 'safe' (exposure) memory with a retrieval cue such as a wristband that clients can then wear and use as cue to recall that memory <ref type="bibr">(Craske, Treanor, Conway, Zbozinek, & Vervliet, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Our model can explain why these interventions work.
Specifically, it suggests that these interventions strengthen the safe memory and thus counteract selective maintenance of 'dangerous' memories.
While the model predicts these interventions prevent dangerous memories from spontaneously resurfacing over time, the 'dangerous' memory may still resurface if it is triggered directly.
The model's predictions also give rise to two novel interventions to eliminate the effect of selective maintenance altogether (and thus prevent relapse).

First, cognitive restructuring focusing on reducing "black-and-white thinking" prior to exposure therapy may change deterministic beliefs (i.e., increase α obs ) and help prevent inference of a new latent cause during exposure therapy (Smith et al., 2021).
text.formatted: First, cognitive restructuring focusing on reducing "black-and-white thinking" prior to exposure therapy may change deterministic beliefs (i.e., increase α obs ) and help prevent inference of a new latent cause during exposure therapy <ref type="bibr">(Smith et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Second, selective maintenance of aversive memories might result from negative self schemas (Dalgleish & Hitchcock, 2023), which may bias sampling from memories towards aversive events.
text.formatted: Second, selective maintenance of aversive memories might result from negative self schemas <ref type="bibr">(Dalgleish & Hitchcock, 2023)</ref>, which may bias sampling from memories towards aversive events.

text.text: Schema therapy (Young, Klosko, & Weishaar, 2006) offers a host of interventions to reduce negative self-schemas, including cognitive, emotional and behavioral techniques.
text.formatted: Schema therapy <ref type="bibr">(Young, Klosko, & Weishaar, 2006)</ref> offers a host of interventions to reduce negative self-schemas, including cognitive, emotional and behavioral techniques.

text.text: Addressing negative self-schemas prior to (or even after) exposure might also prevent later return of fear.

To test our prediction that interfering with any of the mechanisms involved in spontaneous recovery (possibly through the above mentioned interventions) can causally reduce spontaneous recovery, we simulated the influence of each mechanism in turn by changing parameter values in line with the hypothesized effect of the intervention, and generated new data from the modified model to examine whether this change would, in fact, reduce spontaneous recovery.
Figure 11 shows such simulations for one example participant from our exploratory dataset, demonstrating that spontaneous recovery could be prevented by all four interventions.

text.text: Supplementary Figure 6 further elucidates the mechanism underlying the simulated behavior by showing that fear does not return after using a retrieval cue or spacing extinction trials due to relative strengthening of the "safe" memory, while the mechanism underlying the simulated effect of schema therapy is weakening of the acquisition memory.

text.text: We would like to note that we outline here a set of hypotheses on how interventions may be improved, which can serve to inform new empirical studies.

However, empirical support of several of these ideas is still lacking and we do not recommend their implementation during treatment prior to rigorous testing (but see Craske, Treanor, Zbozinek, and Vervliet (2022) for an overview on how to improve exposure therapy).
