text.text: Here, we developed and tested a suite of computational models to understand why fear returns with time, and to quantify individual differences that can differentiate those who go on to show spontaneous recovery of fear from those who do not.

By fitting different computational models to a large dataset, we showed that spontaneous recovery requires a process that strengthens aversive memories over time -leading us to propose selective maintenance of aversive (from here "dangerous") latent causes as a mechanism for spontaneous recovery.

Models that included such selective maintenance provided the best quantitative fit to three datasets, and were the only models that qualitatively captured the differential spontaneous recovery seen in our behavioral fear conditioning task.

Other proposed mechanisms, such as temporal weighting (Devenport, 1998), increased salience of aversive events, or loss of processing of stimuli with repeated exposure (Pavlov, 1927), could not capture differential spontaneous recovery in our dataset.
text.formatted: Other proposed mechanisms, such as temporal weighting <ref type="bibr">(Devenport, 1998)</ref>, increased salience of aversive events, or loss of processing of stimuli with repeated exposure <ref type="bibr">(Pavlov, 1927)</ref>, could not capture differential spontaneous recovery in our dataset.

text.text: There were significant individual differences in our empirical data, with some participants showing spontaneous recovery of fear, and some showing other patterns of responses.

In additional analyses, we showed that the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model-the model that best explained participants who showed spontaneous recovery-could also account for the behavior of the other subgroups of participants, including participants who did not show spontaneous recovery of expectations of the scream US over time, participants who generalized across CS+ and CS-stimuli during acquisition, and participants who over time went back to predicting a scream US for both CS+ and CS-as they did at the start of the task.

We replicated these results across our exploratory dataset, our preregistered replication in a dataset from the general population, and a dataset from a separate study focusing on participants with symptoms of depression.

Supporting our suggestion that the mechanisms identified by our model are relevant for anxiety disorder, we showed through exploratory analyses that that a model parameter quantifying the degree to which participants tend to generalize across the CS+ and CS-in our task correlated with symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder in the latter dataset and that the extent to which participants maintained aversive memories more was associated with traumarelated symptoms.
We further illustrated that the model makes a set of predictions on how we can improve exposure interventions to prevent the return of fear.
In our experiment, we elicited both explicit expectation of the scream US (which were analyzed in the results presented here), as well as affective ratings for each of the CSs.
We saw a similar pattern of responses for affective ratings as we did for expectancy across all four groups.
This included not only spontaneous recovery after extinction, but also significant differences in affective ratings between the SR and No SR groups throughout the phases of the task (Suppl.
Fig. 2), similar to what we found for expectancies (Fig. 3).
text.formatted: Fig. <ref type="figure">2</ref>), similar to what we found for expectancies (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">3</ref>).

text.text: As such, we believe our findings are not limited to explicitly elicited expectancies, but also to emotional processes such as fear.
The degree to which this pattern of results also generalizes to physiological measures in our specific paradigms remains to be investigated.
Prior work has shown that automatic fear responses such as the skin conductance response (SCR) often correlate with individuals' subjective reports of fear (Constantinou et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Prior work has shown that automatic fear responses such as the skin conductance response (SCR) often correlate with individuals' subjective reports of fear <ref type="bibr">(Constantinou et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, accumulating evidence suggests that these measures also reflect partially distinct neural processes.

For example, objective physiological responses are primarily linked to activity within defensive survival circuits involving the amygdala and insula, whereas the conscious experience of fear is thought to rely more on higher-order cortical processes (Taschereau-Dumouchel, Kawato, & Lau, 2020).
text.formatted: For example, objective physiological responses are primarily linked to activity within defensive survival circuits involving the amygdala and insula, whereas the conscious experience of fear is thought to rely more on higher-order cortical processes (Taschereau-Dumouchel, Kawato, & Lau, 2020).

text.text: For the purposes of the present study, subjective ratings provided a particularly informative index as in extinction learning, US-expectancy ratings have been shown to predict post-extinction negative affect, a clinically relevant outcome associated with the return of fear, while SCR measures do not show this relationship (Constantinou et al., 2021).
text.formatted: For the purposes of the present study, subjective ratings provided a particularly informative index as in extinction learning, US-expectancy ratings have been shown to predict post-extinction negative affect, a clinically relevant outcome associated with the return of fear, while SCR measures do not show this relationship <ref type="bibr">(Constantinou et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Given that a major goal of our research is to improve psychological interventions as measured by clinically relevant changes in fear-related cognitions and experiences, these findings support the use of explicit measures.
A major burden of anxiety disorders comes from relapses and recurrences of symptoms even after remission (Batelaan et al., 2017; van Dis et al., 2020).
text.formatted: A major burden of anxiety disorders comes from relapses and recurrences of symptoms even after remission <ref type="bibr">(Batelaan et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">van Dis et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Given our findings, we propose selective maintenance of aversive experiences in memory as a novel mechanism that might contribute to this phenomenon.
To our knowledge, current psychological interventions do not explicitly or purposefully target this mechanism.
Importantly, a mechanistic understanding of why fear might return with time allows us to derive interventions that can prevent this return.

In particular, we proposed several methods that can mitigate the return of fear, each targeting one of the necessary components of spontaneous recovery of fear in our model: cognitive restructuring, using retrieval cues, spacing extinction/exposure sessions and schema therapy.
Simulations of the hypothesized intervention effects confirmed a reduction of spontaneous recovery (at least in the model).
Our next step is to test these predictions in a clinical trial.
As such, our work might lay the foundation for psychological interventions derived from computational principles.
In a recent perspective paper (Berwian, Hitchock, Pisupati, Schoen, & Niv, 2025), we provided an introduction to this approach, along with examples, for a broader audience that includes clinicians.
text.formatted: In a recent perspective paper <ref type="bibr">(Berwian, Hitchock, Pisupati, Schoen, & Niv, 2025)</ref>, we provided an introduction to this approach, along with examples, for a broader audience that includes clinicians.

text.text: Mechanistic insights from the model explain phenomena of anxiety Next, we discuss how our hypothesised mechanism of selective maintenance of aversive events, which results in a relative strengthening of dangerous memories or context inferences compared to safe ones, may explain a range of phenomena related to anxiety, including overgeneralisation, the development of anxiety, and intolerance of uncertainty.

A commonly observed phenomenon in individuals with anxiety disorders is overgeneralization (Cooper et al., 2022), i.e., generalization of learned expectations from a few negative experiences to many (new) situations and contexts.
text.formatted: A commonly observed phenomenon in individuals with anxiety disorders is overgeneralization <ref type="bibr">(Cooper et al., 2022)</ref>, i.e., generalization of learned expectations from a few negative experiences to many (new) situations and contexts.

text.text: Based on our computational framework, we propose that there are at least two possibly distinct types of overgeneralization.
The first type involves a failure to distinguish between stimuli.
This resembles the behavior observed in the Generalizers group, resulting from the inference of mainly a single latent cause that accounts for different observations.

In a previous experiment in which we tested generalization of US predictions to (previously unseen) stimuli spanning the perceptual range between the CS+ and the CS-(Aitsahalia, 2022), we indeed showed that the behavior of participants from the Generalizers group in the generalization test closely resembles the pattern of 'overgeneralization' proposed by Cooper et al. (2022).
text.formatted: In a previous experiment in which we tested generalization of US predictions to (previously unseen) stimuli spanning the perceptual range between the CS+ and the CS-(Aitsahalia, 2022), we indeed showed that the behavior of participants from the Generalizers group in the generalization test closely resembles the pattern of 'overgeneralization' proposed by <ref type="bibr">Cooper et al. (2022)</ref>.

text.text: Inferring a single latent cause for distinct stimuli could lead to fear of many situations and stimuli also associated with that same latent cause.
(In principle, this type of overgeneralization does not need to be biased to negative experience, but could be in case of increased salience of aversive events.)

Interestingly, behavior resulting from the inference of a single latent cause (due to stochastic priors in the Generalizers group) aligns with the main criterion of generalized anxiety disorder according to the DSM-5: "Excessive anxiety and worry (apprehensive expectation), occurring more days than not for at least 6 months, about a number of events or activities" (emphasis ours).

In line with the model's prediction that stochastic priors can drive generalized anxiety symptoms, in our sample with internalizing symptoms we found that participants who were fit with more stochastic priors tended to have more symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder.
We note that for people showing this type of generalization, extinction is expected to occur slowly but should eventually be successful.

Although this extinction is likely to be resistant to the return of fear, its gradual pace may be misinterpreted as a lack of response to exposure therapy, thereby resulting in its premature termination.
Our model predicts that exposure therapy will show its effects faster when latent causes are more distinctly separated.

Thus, to facilitate separation, interventions can promote attention to differences between stimuli or situations, such as is done in interpersonal discrimination exercises (McCullough, Schramm, & Penberthy, 2014).
text.formatted: Thus, to facilitate separation, interventions can promote attention to differences between stimuli or situations, such as is done in interpersonal discrimination exercises <ref type="bibr">(McCullough, Schramm, & Penberthy, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: A second alternative type of overgeneralization that is specific to negative events can simply result from selective maintenance of such events.

Selective maintenance would make the latent causes (memories) that involve aversive events stronger with time, such that they carry more weight when an individual is confronted with an even remotely similar situation.
That is, due to the strength of the latent cause, it will be a priori likely to be inferred in many different situations.
The development of anxiety.

In line with suggestions in the literature (e.g., Gagne, Dayan, & Bishop, 2018), selective maintenance of aversive experiences in memory can explain the development of anxiety disorders (including post traumatic stress disorder) after an exceptionally aversive event due to increased reactivation of the memory of the aversive ("dangerous") event.
text.formatted: In line with suggestions in the literature (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Gagne, Dayan, & Bishop, 2018)</ref>, selective maintenance of aversive experiences in memory can explain the development of anxiety disorders (including post traumatic stress disorder) after an exceptionally aversive event due to increased reactivation of the memory of the aversive ("dangerous") event.

text.text: With time, the aversive memory overshadows "safe" memories of similar situations without aversive outcomes, even if the safe events had occurred more frequently than the dangerous event.
Avoidance behavior further facilitates the memory imbalance in favor of the "dangerous" memory, as it prevents new non-aversive experiences that would strengthen the "safe" memory.
As such, a vicious cycle of reactivation and avoidance can lead to the development of an anxiety disorder or post-traumatic stress disorder.
This prediction aligns with our exploratory finding that symptoms of traumatic reactions were correlated with larger estimates of the effect of selective maintenance in our undifferentiated sample.
Note, however, that this result needs to be interpreted with caution and further tested, ideally with a more symptomatic sample.
Intolerance of uncertainty in anxiety.
Difficulties in tolerating uncertainty have recently been proposed as a theory of anxiety.
Brown, Price, and Dombrovski (2023) reviewed a series of studies suggesting that deficits in dealing with uncertainty are more prevalent in anxiety than are exaggerated fear of aversive events.

This aligns with the effect of selective maintenance of aversive memories, which can provide a causal explanation for how aberrant behavior in the face of uncertainty comes about in individuals with anxiety.
The idea is that uncertainty about the occurrence of aversive outcomes will have led to forming both a "safe" and a "dangerous" latent cause.

Selective maintenance then increases the relative strength of the "dangerous" latent cause, leading to higher estimates of aversive outcomes in such situations, similar to the overestimation of the probability of a scream in acquisition that we saw in the SR group.
In contrast, in situations with certain aversive outcomes, selective maintenance would have no effect and would not predict different behavior for individuals with anxiety.
Alternative models.
The potential model space and combination of mechanisms is, of course, endless.

For clarity and comprehensibility, we reported here a set of models that represent either key distinct hypotheses from the literature or our own hypotheses that we considered biologically and psychologically plausible.
In the Suppl.
Subsec.

2.3, we provide an overview of further alternative modeling frameworks (reinforcement learning), theories (temporal context and response fatigue) and other versions of our own models and describe why they fail to account for our data.
These alternative models were either unable to generate differential spontaneous recovery or they did not capture the empirical data better than the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model.
Nevertheless, we cannot exclude that other formalizations or interpretations of these or other alternative mechanisms can account for spontaneous recovery of fear.

For example, our current formalization and data cannot differentiate between selective maintenance of aversive events and faster decay rates of inhibitory associations as proposed by Paskewitz, Stoddard, and Jones (2022).
text.formatted: For example, our current formalization and data cannot differentiate between selective maintenance of aversive events and faster decay rates of inhibitory associations as proposed by <ref type="bibr">Paskewitz, Stoddard, and Jones (2022)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, it is likely that different mechanisms are at play in different individuals and that the observed behavior results from a combination of mechanisms.

We note that our conclusions are also limited by the (relatively) small amount of data we had in two aspects: First, we had few data points (ratings) per participant and used only one data type (expectancy ratings).

Because we used principles of parsimony that seek to identify the simplest model that explains the data (i.e., we penalized models for their free parameters; Wilson & Collins, 2019), we may have missed more complex processes (e.g., additional temporal organizations of context) that would only become visible when additional data, for instance from direct measurements of memory, are also assessed.
text.formatted: Because we used principles of parsimony that seek to identify the simplest model that explains the data (i.e., we penalized models for their free parameters; <ref type="bibr">Wilson & Collins, 2019)</ref>, we may have missed more complex processes (e.g., additional temporal organizations of context) that would only become visible when additional data, for instance from direct measurements of memory, are also assessed.

text.text: Second, we had only one trial per participant to measure spontaneous recovery.

This not only makes it challenging to estimate spontaneous recovery reliably, but also poses a challenge for model comparison because the single trial can only provide limited support for models that specifically capture spontaneous recovery.

In this respect, the fact that models with selective maintenance won when penalized for extra parameters shows that this process was important not only for spontaneous recovery, but rather had signatures throughout the learning process.
Improving measurement accuracy.
While our findings were robust and replicated across datasets, most effect sizes were small to medium.
Additionally, model fits at the individual level revealed that our model did not fully capture the extent of spontaneous recovery in all participants.
This may be due to different mechanisms underlying spontaneous recovery across individuals, as previously discussed.

Alternatively, the variability could result from noise in the data or limitations in the fitting procedure, which may not always recover optimal parameter estimates given the stochastic nature of the model.

Increasing the number of trials and applying hierarchical modeling approaches could improve the robustness of parameter estimation, thereby enhancing the precision of measuring these mechanisms in individuals.

On a different note, Lonsdorf and Merz (2017) suggest that new advanced statistical approaches are needed to capture individual response trajectories and advance individual-difference research on fear conditioning.
text.formatted: On a different note, <ref type="bibr">Lonsdorf and Merz (2017)</ref> suggest that new advanced statistical approaches are needed to capture individual response trajectories and advance individual-difference research on fear conditioning.

text.text: Our model captures entire trajectories of CS+ and CS-responses across four different phases and many individual trials with only 3-4 parameters (while avoiding noisy difference of differences scores), and, therefore, we hope it will be a useful tool for this type of research as well as for further mental health investigations.
Alternative task design.

While our pre-registered replication and additional replication in a symptomatic sample give confidence that our model was not overfit to a specific dataset, the model could nevertheless be too specific to our task design and thus not generalize to other versions of this paradigm.
For instance, the amount of spontaneous recovery in our paradigm could be triggered by the specific sequence of reinforced and non-reinforced trials, which was identical across participants.
Reassuringly, we previously observed similar patterns of behavior in other versions of the task with different numbers and sequences of trials in acquisition and extinction.

We specifically note that most fear conditioning paradigms test for spontaneous recovery after 24h or longer (Lonsdorf et al., 2017), to allow for memory consolidation prior to the test, which we did not do here.
text.formatted: We specifically note that most fear conditioning paradigms test for spontaneous recovery after 24h or longer <ref type="bibr">(Lonsdorf et al., 2017)</ref>, to allow for memory consolidation prior to the test, which we did not do here.

text.text: However, in several pilot studies and in a separate full experiment (N=441), we did test for spontaneous recovery in a separate session ˜24h after the acquisition and extinction session.
In all these experiments, we found a similar pattern of behavior across all subgroups (data not shown as the full study is still in progress).

Interestingly, and in line with the predictions of our selective maintenance model, with the longer delay before the spontaneous recovery test, we observed more differential spontaneous recovery in the SR group (which is predicted because the longer interval provides more time for the effect of selective maintenance to unfold).
Furthermore, a greater proportion of participants showed behavior consistent with a "Return to Start" in the spontaneous recovery test, i.e., 50% expectation of a scream for both CS+ and CS-.
This is predicted by our model due to more decay of existing memories over the long delay time, which leads to inference of new latent causes at test.

Formally, our model accounted for this phenomenon in the data from the Return to Start group either through the formation of new latent causes for the CS+ and the CSin the spontaneous recovery test, or through a return of the "dangerous" latent cause for the CS+ and the formation of a new latent cause for the CS-.
Data from the present paradigm cannot tease these different latent cause inferences apart.

Similarly, data from participants in the Generalizers group may not contain sufficient information to reliably estimate decay, selective maintenance and low salience parameters, as changes in the strength of different latent causes have no visible impact on behavior when only one latent cause is inferred.
Thus, participants from these two groups were not included in analyses of the selective maintenance parameter.
Interpreting associations between parameter estimates and symptoms of anxiety.

As mentioned above, and in line with our hypotheses that stochastic priors might underlie overgeneralisation in anxiety and that selective maintenance could drive the development of anxiety after aversive experiences, we found small positive correlations between the prior over observations and symptoms of generalised anxiety, as well as between selective maintenance and symptoms of traumatic reactions.

As we carefully followed proposed procedures to avoid spurious correlations between task measures and symptoms, such as screening out inattentive responders in self-report and task measures (Zorowitz & Niv, 2023), and employed robust statistical approaches to prevent the influence of outliers, we likely avoided false positives.
text.formatted: As we carefully followed proposed procedures to avoid spurious correlations between task measures and symptoms, such as screening out inattentive responders in self-report and task measures <ref type="bibr">(Zorowitz & Niv, 2023)</ref>, and employed robust statistical approaches to prevent the influence of outliers, we likely avoided false positives.

text.text: However, we would like to note that these were exploratory analyses and the effects we found are small and need to be interpreted with caution.
Furthermore, for each study, we analysed the anxiety measures collected alongside the task data.
However, depending on the goals of each study, those studies did not necessarily broadly assess anxiety and other psychopathology dimensions.

The association between effective selective maintenance estimates (ω ′ ) and traumatic reaction symptoms survived after controlling for many other anxiety symptom scales, including generalised anxiety symptoms.

This provides support for our hypothesis that selective maintenance is relevant for the development and maintenance of anxiety, and is specific to anxiety that is related to experiencing aversive events.

However, because in the sample with internalizing symptoms we examined only bivariate associations between generalised anxiety symptoms (GAD7) and parameter estimates of the prior (a obs ), we cannot determine whether these results are specific to generalised anxiety symptoms.

While our two-stage modeling approach aligns with common practice and recommendations in the literature (Friston, Stephan, Lund, Morcom, & Kiebel, 2005) and is more computationally feasible than more sophisticated hierarchical methods, we may have missed relationships that the latter may have detected.
text.formatted: While our two-stage modeling approach aligns with common practice and recommendations in the literature <ref type="bibr">(Friston, Stephan, Lund, Morcom, & Kiebel, 2005)</ref> and is more computationally feasible than more sophisticated hierarchical methods, we may have missed relationships that the latter may have detected.

text.text: Future work could, for example, follow the proposed HiTOP methods of deriving latent factors underlying psychopathology using the full HiTOP structure measure (Simms et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Future work could, for example, follow the proposed HiTOP methods of deriving latent factors underlying psychopathology using the full HiTOP structure measure <ref type="bibr">(Simms et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These factors could then be related to parameter estimates to increase sensitivity to detecting relationships between model parameters and symptomology (Cooper, Perkins, Webler, Dunsmoor, & Krueger, 2024) and to assess whether model parameters are related to anxiety symptoms specifically or to internalizing symptoms more broadly (Watson, Levin-Aspenson, et al., 2022).
text.formatted: These factors could then be related to parameter estimates to increase sensitivity to detecting relationships between model parameters and symptomology <ref type="bibr">(Cooper, Perkins, Webler, Dunsmoor, & Krueger, 2024)</ref> and to assess whether model parameters are related to anxiety symptoms specifically or to internalizing symptoms more broadly <ref type="bibr">(Watson, Levin-Aspenson, et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This analytic method could be further improved by a joint model that simultaneously estimates parameters at the subject level and their association with psychopathology.
Extension to other return-of-fear phenomena.
Two other return-of-fear phenomena are often observed after fear conditioning and extinction.

These include the return of fear when returning to the acquisition context (if acquisition and extinction occurred in different contexts) or when switching to a completely new context ('renewal'), and after re-exposure to the US alone ('reinstatement').
Both phenomena have been proposed to result from the reactivation of the acquisition context (e.g., Bouton (1993)).
text.formatted: Both phenomena have been proposed to result from the reactivation of the acquisition context (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Bouton (1993)</ref>).

text.text: Future research can empirically test predictions from context theories and the selective maintenance hypothesis to see which observed phenomena can be better explained either by context theories or by the selective maintenance hypothesis, or by a combination of both.
We propose selective maintenance of aversive memories as a key mechanism underlying spontaneous recovery of fear after extinction.
Models incorporating this process explained the behavioral data across multiple datasets, outperforming alternative theories.
These models also provided mechanistic insights into overgeneralization and the development of anxiety.
These insights were empirically supported by correlations between parameter estimates quantifying the proposed mechanisms and symptoms of anxiety.

These results may have clinical implications: targeting mechanisms supporting selective maintenance, for example through cognitive interventions or spaced extinction, may help reduce the risk of relapse after successful treatment.

While further research is needed to test these clinical predictions and the model's neural basis, selective maintenance of aversive memories offers a unified, testable account of the development, persistence and return of anxiety, and how the influence of selective maintenance might be effectively modified. upon request.

This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Princeton University (Protocol 11968), and all participants provided written informed consent.
Participants were recruited from Prolific to complete a series of studies including online behavioral tasks and mental health questionnaires in spring 2023.
All participants were compensated for their time at a rate of $13/hr.
To qualify for the study, participants had to reside in the United States, Canada, Australia, or New Zealand, be fluent in English, and have headphones.

We first report the analyses of the first half of that dataset with N = 376 participants, which were labeled an 'exploration dataset.' (Later, we will report replication of our findings in the second half of the dataset.)
From the exploration dataset, 23 participants were excluded due to incomplete datasets and 37 participants were excluded due to failing more than two audio attention checks.
The final dataset contained N = 316 participants.
Information on the distribution of self-reported sex in this sample is presented in Suppl.
Tab 1.
We designed an online-administered aversive conditioning and extinction task (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: We designed an online-administered aversive conditioning and extinction task (Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: On each trial, participants saw a face-down card that then "flipped over" to reveal one of two stimuli: a moon with three stars (CS+) or three candles (CS-).
Participants then had to press the space bar to reveal the trial's outcome, described in the instructions as "the sound associated with that stimulus".
On some CS+ trials, this was an aversive but tolerable auditory scream (US; see below), and for all other trials there was no outcome.
The task was completely Pavlovian; key pressing allowed reaction-time measurements and ensured continued attention to CSs, but did not otherwise affect the occurrence of the US.
The sequence of a trial was as follows: a card appeared face-down for 500 ms and then flipped over (this animation lasted 100 ms).
An event listener was then activated and the participant had 6000 ms to press the space bar before the trial timed out.
If the participant failed to respond in time, a warning message was displayed for 3000 ms, after which the trial was repeated.
If the space bar was pressed and the stimulus had an associated sound, a delay of between 300-800 ms occurred before the audio was played.
This jitter was randomly generated on each trial and was introduced to prevent participants from precisely anticipating the timing of the outcome.
After the space bar was pressed, the card flipped back over and flew off the screen to indicate the end of the trial (this animation lasted 500 ms, regardless of whether a sound was played).
We used three aversive audio clips across trials.
They were edited to be of similar volume and duration (2000 ms).
Every three trials, on average, participants were asked to rate how likely they expected each of the two CSs would be followed by a scream on a scale of 0-100% using two horizontal slider bars.
The sliders were initialized in a random location and each had to be moved to continue to the next trial.
Participants completed 31 ratings for each CS.

Within these, two sets of ratings that followed previous ratings without new trials or significant passage of time since the previous rating were excluded from analyses, leaving 29 ratings per CS per participant.
One rating was always completed before each phase.
In addition, about every 8-10 trials, participants rated their feeling when viewing each of the stimuli on a horizontal slider bar ranging from calm to alert ("affective ratings" hereafter).
The task consisted of 4 phases.
In the acquisition phase (26 trials), 50% of 16 CS+ trials were followed by a US (total: 8 screams), and the CS-appeared on 10 trials.

This phase was followed by a 3-5 minute break in which participants completed a filler questionnaire of no interest (the 20-item short form International Personality Item Pool-Five-Factor Model measure; Donnellan, Oswald, Baird, & Lucas, 2006).
text.formatted: This phase was followed by a 3-5 minute break in which participants completed a filler questionnaire of no interest (the 20-item short form International Personality Item Pool-Five-Factor Model measure; <ref type="bibr">Donnellan, Oswald, Baird, & Lucas, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: The extinction phase included 30 trials, 18 CS+, 12 CS-, with no US.

Next, participants completed a separate task (a risky decision making task in which they made choices between a sure 5-point reward and a stimulus with an unknown but learnable chance of giving 10 points or 0 points; not analyzed here) for ∼15 minutes.
This was followed by a spontaneous recovery test (16 trials, 10 CS+ and 6 CS-; no US), and then a relearning phase (10 CS+ with 4 USs; 6 CS-).
All participants saw the same sequence of CSs and USs and were asked to provide ratings between the same trials (see Suppl.
Sub.
1.1 for the order of trials and other technical details).
We note that participants intentionally first encountered the CS+ stimulus without reinforcement in the acquisition phase.

We chose this design to mimic the fact that in real life encounters with aversive outcomes often follow similar stimuli in non-aversive contexts, and to ensure the latent cause associated with the CS+ but no aversive outcome (often labeled the "inhibitory memory" in the literature) is inferred first and there is no "primacy advantage" to the aversive latent cause that could account for its spontaneous recovery over time.

As participants were tested online and from remotely, to ensure they heard the US loudly enough and did not reduce the volume throughout the task, participants completed a set of volume calibration steps and six auditory attention checks were spread throughout the task (see Suppl.
Subsec.
Including the two breaks, the task took approximately 50 min.

We used a partial reinforcement rate (50%) in line with other fear conditioning paradigms (as reviewed for example by Lonsdorf et al. (2017)) and to make our experimental setting more naturalistic, since it is unlikely that people who develop anxietyrelated disorders experienced a 100% rate of aversive experiences.
text.formatted: We used a partial reinforcement rate (50%) in line with other fear conditioning paradigms (as reviewed for example by <ref type="bibr">Lonsdorf et al. (2017)</ref>) and to make our experimental setting more naturalistic, since it is unlikely that people who develop anxietyrelated disorders experienced a 100% rate of aversive experiences.

text.text: Partial reinforcement also reduces working memory effects that can masquerade as learning (Collins & Frank, 2012) and introduces uncertainty about outcomes, which might be important for anxiety disorders (Brown et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Partial reinforcement also reduces working memory effects that can masquerade as learning <ref type="bibr">(Collins & Frank, 2012)</ref> and introduces uncertainty about outcomes, which might be important for anxiety disorders <ref type="bibr">(Brown et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In two separate online sessions, participants completed the GAD7 questionnaire (prior to completing the task; Spitzer, Kroenke, Williams, and Löwe (2006); Löwe et al. (2008)), several subscales of the HiTOP questionnaire (several weeks after completing the task; Watson, Forbes, et al. (2022)), as well as other symptom self-report questionnaires not analyzed here.

text.text: GAD7 is among the most commonly used self-report questionnaires for anxiety and recommended or required by many funding agencies to allow comparing or pooling of data from different studies.
It primarily captures symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder with 7 questions rated on a scale from 0-3.
Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) measures aim at assessing psychopathology with a dimensional approach (Kotov et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) measures aim at assessing psychopathology with a dimensional approach <ref type="bibr">(Kotov et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: As we were interested in many specific anxieties, for the analyses reported here, we examined data from the following HiTOP subscales: social anxiety subscale (15 items), the agoraphobia subscale (6 items), animal phobia (6 items), situational phobia (6 items), traumatic reactions subscale (8 items), depression/anxiety (15), compulsivity (15), situational phobia (5), blood-injection phobia (3), panic (6) and separation insecurity (6), as well as GAD7.

These items were selected based on the recommendations of the HiTOP consortium based on preliminary testing (Watson, Forbes, et al., 2022) and to maximize content overlap with several standard anxiety scales.
text.formatted: These items were selected based on the recommendations of the HiTOP consortium based on preliminary testing <ref type="bibr">(Watson, Forbes, et al., 2022)</ref> and to maximize content overlap with several standard anxiety scales.

Subsec.
1.2 for further information and a list of items for each subscale.
Participants were invited to complete the HiTOP questions up to several weeks after completing the task.
However, we note that participants were instructed to indicate for each statement "Have there been significant times during the last 12 months in which the following statements applied to you?"
which also covered the period of completing the task.
Responses were recorded on the following scale: (0) Not at all, (1) A little, (2) Moderately, (3) A lot.

To verify that behavioral differences in the task were not driven by different usage of the expectancy rating scale (i.e., differences in people's response style), we added two types of response style measures.

First, we created five anchoring vignettes, in which we described the number of neutral and aversive stimuli observed by another person and asked participants to indicate how that person should rate the expectancy of negative outcomes (Hopkins & King, 2010).
text.formatted: First, we created five anchoring vignettes, in which we described the number of neutral and aversive stimuli observed by another person and asked participants to indicate how that person should rate the expectancy of negative outcomes <ref type="bibr">(Hopkins & King, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Second, we asked participants to rate the likelihood of four events such as "How likely is it that the sun will rise tomorrow?".
The scenarios were chosen such that no expert knowledge was required or would influence the rating, and such that ratings would represent participants' responding across the range of probabilities.
One goal was to test whether some participants did not use the whole scale even for expectations of "never" or "always".
For both measures, we computed the mean and variance of each participant's ratings.
All questions are available in Suppl.
Subsec.
In our pilot data, we observed that most participants showed distinct patterns of behavioral features that suggested they could be categorized into different groups.
In parallel, simulations with our model prior to fitting it to any data also indicated that these behavioral features can arise from different mechanistic functions.

To provide statistical evidence for the hypotheses emerging from simulations, we therefore decided on the below criteria to separate individuals into four subgroups a priori and included the same criteria in our preregistration of the replication dataset.

Specifically, we categorized participants into four subgroups: N = 13 participants who showed similar expectations for the CS+ and CS-at the end of acquisition (< 10 points difference on a scale from 0 to 100%) were categorized into the 'Generalizers' group.
text.formatted: Specifically, we categorized participants into four subgroups: N = 13 participants who showed similar expectations for the CS+ and CS-at the end of acquisition (< 10 points difference on a scale from 0 to 100%) were categorized into the 'Generalizers' group.

text.text: The remaining participants were then categorized into groups based on their behavior on the spontaneous recovery test, in particular, their first rating of expectation of a scream for both the CS+ and the CS-, which occurred immediately at the beginning of the spontaneous recovery test phase before any other exposure to the stimuli or screams or audio instructions.

N = 175 participants who increased their expectation of the US by more than 10 points compared to the end of extinction for the CS+ but not for the CS-were categorized into the 'spontaneous recovery' ('SR') group-a group that includes participants who show differential spontaneous recovery, i.e., an increase in their CS+ rating without a substantial increase in their CS-rating in the spontaneous recovery test.

N = 88 participants whose expectations for both stimuli increased by at most 10 points were categorized into the 'No SR' group (we used a change in expectation of 10 points as a cutoff for distinguishing between No SR and SR to account for random response noise), and N = 37 participants whose expectations increased by more than 10 points for both stimuli were categorized into the 'Return to Start' group.
N = 3 participants who did not meet any of these criteria were not included in subgroup analyses.

Most of our analyses focused on the SR and No SR groups, as differences between these groups were of main interest to understand the mechanism of spontaneous recovery, and these were also the largest groups, which allowed us to identify robust group differences.

First, in a set of model-agnostic analyses, we tested whether the SR and No SR groups showed different behavioral features throughout the task (beyond the differences in the SR test phase, by which these groups were defined) by comparing 1) their a priori expectations of negative outcomes for the CS+ and CS-(i.e., their first expectancy ratings); 2) their acquisition learning, measured as the mean differential ratings for the CS+ minus CS-in the remaining ratings from the acquisition phase; 3) the effect of the first (short) break, by comparing the change in expectancy ratings for the CS+ minus CS-in the first rating after the break minus the last rating before the break; 4) the extent to which expectations of the US decreased during the extinction phase in each group, measured as the difference between the first and last ratings for the CS+ minus the CS-in the extinction phase; 5) their differential spontaneous recovery, by comparing the change in CS+ minus CS-ratings between the end of extinction and the beginning of the spontaneous recovery test; and 6) their rate of reacquisiton, by comparing the change in CS+ minus CS-ratings from the last rating of the spontaneous recovery test phase to the last rating of the relearning phase.
We repeated these analyses for the affective ratings with the exception of the effect of the first short break as we did not measure affective ratings immediately after that break.
For a similar reason, we also used the affective rating after acquisition rather than the first rating of extinction to measure the effect of extinction (number 4 above).
Next, we formalized learning of the latent structure of the task using Bayesian nonparametric models of latent cause inference (Gershman et al., 2015; Gershman & Blei, 2012).
text.formatted: Next, we formalized learning of the latent structure of the task using Bayesian nonparametric models of latent cause inference <ref type="bibr">(Gershman et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gershman & Blei, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In the latent cause framework, observations (here, trials) are attributed to one of an unlimited number of latent causes L t ∈ [1, ..., j], each with its own unique set of parameters Φ j = {φ j,i } that determine probabilities of observing each of i ∈ [1 : 4] features.

We set i=1 to indicate the CS-, i=2 the CS+, i=3 a 'break stimulus' (to model the time between acquisition and extinction and between extinction and spontaneous recovery test) and i=4 to indicate the US.
Thus, in our models, each latent cause embodies a different association-different probabilities of observing the CSs and US.
An infinite-capacity prior over latent causes can flexibly add new causes when they are necessary to explain dissimilar observations.

We use a Chinese Restaurant Process (CRP) prior (Aldous et al., 1985) that expects latent cause L t+1 on trial t + 1 to be a previously encountered or a new latent cause with probabilities as follows: if j is a new latent cause where N j,t is the number of observations generated by latent cause number j up to trial t (see more below) and α ≥ 0 is a parameter that influences the probability of new latent causes.
text.formatted: We use a Chinese Restaurant Process (CRP) prior <ref type="bibr">(Aldous et al., 1985)</ref> that expects latent cause L t+1 on trial t + 1 to be a previously encountered or a new latent cause with probabilities as follows: if j is a new latent cause where N j,t is the number of observations generated by latent cause number j up to trial t (see more below) and α ≥ 0 is a parameter that influences the probability of new latent causes.

text.text: (Note that there is some non-zero probability of a new latent cause on every trial, hence the number of previous latent causes on trial t + 1 is t.
Also, while in some models Σ t m=1 N m,t = t, this is not the case in all our models below, hence we spell out the sum explicitly in the denominator.)

Conditional on latent cause j having been drawn for trial t + 1, the generative model assumes that observations O t+1 are generated by independent Bernoulli processes with probability φ j,i for each feature i generated by latent cause j, p(O i,t+1 |L t+1 = j) = φ j,i (t + 1).
When a new latent cause j is initialized, initial probabilities φ j,i are drawn from Beta priors with two parameters a obs > 0 and b obs > 0.
text.formatted: When a new latent cause j is initialized, initial probabilities φ j,i are drawn from Beta priors with two parameters a obs > 0 and b obs > 0.

text.text: Given that pilot data from the task showed that absent any data, participants' prior expections of a US before the start of the experiment are ∼ 50%, we assumed symmetric Beta priors (a obs = b obs ) whose mean is always 50%.

Values of a obs > 1 imply initial φ j,i that are unimodal around 0.5, with higher a obs being more stochastic (that is, more tightly concentrated around φ j,i = 0.5; Fig. 4A), while smaller a obs result in bimodal φ j,i that are more deterministic (i.e., closer to 0 or 1; Fig. 4C).

The basic model.
Here, N j,t is the number of trials caused by latent cause j up to the trial t.

Since there is a nonzero probability that each of the previous latent causes has generated the current trial, in practice N j,t sums the posterior probability of latent cause j in each trial: N j,t = Σ t ′ ≤t P(L t ′ = j|O 1:t ), where O 1:t are the observations up to trial t.

We fit two versions of this model, a "Basic Concentration Model" with α as the single free parameter and a obs = 1 (i.e., a flat prior over observations given a latent cause), and a "Basic Prior Model" with a obs as the single free parameter and α = 0.03.
The former model has been used previously to model fear acquisition and extinction in a similar paradigm, but not spontaneous recovery (Gershman & Hartley, 2015).

Selective Maintenance Model.

Inspired by evidence that humans remember negative events better (e.g., Rouhani et al., 2023), in this model we hypothesized that latent causes associated with aversive stimuli (here, the scream US) are protected from decay, perhaps due to memory reactivation (Wimmer et al., 2023).

Salience Model.

Emotionally charged stimuli experienced during an event may change the salience of the event, for example, they may capture more attention (see Dolcos et al., 2020, for a review), potentially enhancing memory for the event.

text.text: To account for this salience effect, we implemented a model that counts trials with an aversive US as C ≥ 0 rather than 1 in the counts N j,t :
Note that O 4,t is 1 on trials with a US, and 0 otherwise.

This model reduces to the basic model for C = 1, and ascribes extra salience to trials with aversive events when C > 1, but also allows for lower salience for these trials for0 ≤ C < 1 (we will make use of this case specifically in the two models below).

text.text: In this model, we combined the selective maintenance and salience models, restricting C ≤ 1 (labeled C low hereafter):

In contrast to the selective maintenance model above, in which selective maintenance of "dangerous" latent causes occurs throughout the learning phases and breaks, this model can also capture behavior resulting from selective maintenance occurring only during breaks, because the C low parameter can reduce the amount of updating for trials with aversive outcomes.
In this way, low salience can counteract the effect of selective maintenance during the learning phases.
However, C low has no impact during breaks, where the effect of selective maintenance can fully unfold.
Note that we used C low rather than C to ensure good parameter recoverability, however in our exploration dataset we found similar patterns of results when relaxing this restriction.

Processing Loss Model.

To model the idea that repeated exposure to a stimulus may reduce its processing due to habituation or neural fatigue (Pavlov, 1927), in this model, for each CS, we added observations to the count N j,t according to a decreasing logistic function of how often that CS had been observed so far: where d i,t = 1 1+e -λ(ν+Σ t ′ ≤t O i,t ′ ) and λ ≤ 0 and ν ≥ 0.

text.text: Each time participants were asked to make an expectation rating, the algorithm first inferred the posterior probability over possible partitions of trials into latent causes based on all previous observations plus a current observation of either the CS+ or the CS-and used this inference to generate a prediction of the probability of the US: p(O 4,t = 1|O 1:3,1:t , O 4,1:t-1 , Θ, M) = Σp(O 4,t = 1|L 1:t ) • p(L 1:t |O 1:3,1:t , O 4,1:t-1 , Θ, M) where the sum was over all possible latent cause assignments approximated by averaging across the 1000 particles.
This probability was used to compute the likelihoods of the participant's rating.
No updating occured based on these inferences.
After observing all stimuli in a trial (CSs and USs), the posterior distribution over latent causes was calculated taking all previous observations into account.
This was then used to update the observation probabilities for each latent cause φ j,i .
Throughout, the model observed the same stimuli as the participants.

To simulate breaks, we presented the model with a dummy stimulus O 3 , simulating a short break between acquisition and extinction as 9 trials of O 3 and the long break between extinction and the spontaneous recovery test phase as 34 trials of O 3 .

These numbers of trials were chosen as the approximate number of task trials that would have occurred in the breaks in the experiment, as per the average time it took participants to complete the task trials and the break activities.

text.text: As these nonparametric models are analytically intractable, we used a simulation-based approach to generate predictions of the occurrence of the US (the scream) and estimated parameters by maximizing the likelihood of the participant's ratings assuming the response error was normally distributed around the model prediction.

We computed the standard deviation σ of this normal distribution empirically for each individual as where n is the number of rating data points (with g i, j being the actual rating (guess) number j for stimulus i between 0-100 divided by 100) and p(O 4, j = 1|O i ) was calculated according to equation 10 for each stimulus O i for i ∈ {1, 2} and each rating timepoint j.
We computed the likelihood of each individual expectancy rating g i, j at timepoint t (that is, after trial t -1) for stimulus i ∈ {1, 2} as
Because participants could not register an expectation below 0 or above 100, we added the probability density for ratings below 0 and above 1 to expectancy ratings of 0 and 1, respectively.

Alternative formulations of the response function, such as assuming the response error was distributed according to a beta distribution or fixing or fitting σ, led to very similar fits and the same overall pattern of results.
We used the Bayesian Adaptive Direct Search (BADS; Acerbi & Ma, 2017) algorithm for parameter search, with 24 restarts for each participant and model.

text.text: Importantly, the model-fitting algorithm only received participants' expectation ratings, and no other information about the participant (such as their subgroup categorization).
To identify the winning model, we first computed AIC values for all subjects for all models.
We then subtracted the AIC value of each model from the AIC value of the numerically winning model on a subject-by-subject level.
If the distribution of these differences was significantly below 0, this indicated that the numerically winning model indeed explained the data better.
If the distribution was significantly above 0, this indicated that the other model explained the data better.
Because the distribution of AIC differences can be non-normal and/or skewed, we used bootstrapping to test whether it was significantly different from 0.
Specifically, for each distribution, bootstrap resampling was performed by drawing with replacement samples of size n (equal to the number of participants) from the distribution.
This procedure was repeated 10,000 times.

For each bootstrap sample, we then computed the mean as well as a trimmed mean (the mean of the distribution less the upper and lower 2.5% of values (i.e., a 5% total trim), which provides a measure robust to outliers).

Percentile confidence intervals (95%) for each statistic (mean and trimmed mean) were estimated using the percentile method, defined as the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the corresponding bootstrap distributions. 95% confidence intervals that do not include 0 correspond to a significant result in a two-sided test, therefore, we considered AIC differences where the 95% confidence interval for the bootstrapped samples did not include 0 to indicate the differences were significantly different from zero.

To compute a two-sided bootstrapped p-value that corresponds to the confidence intervals, we counted how many bootstrapped values were on the other side of the null-value (i.e., 0) than the bootstrapped mean and multiplied that count by 2 to mimic a 2-sided test.
As parameter estimates and data ratings were bounded, they could not follow a normal distribution.
Hence, we used non-parametric significance tests for comparisons between subgroups.
For all these tests, we report rank-biserial correlation r as effect size.
As several of our variables were zero-inflated or not normally distributed, we applied Spearman correlations in additional confirmatory analyses to reduce the influence of outliers.
We repeated the model-free analyses of the expectancy ratings (described above) on the simulated data from the winning model.
We added response noise to the simulated data by replacing each simulated data point with a data point drawn from a normal distribution with the data point as µ and the empirically computed σ.
Ratings below 0 and above 1 were assigned to be 0 or 1, respectively.

The goal of this replication was to test whether we can confirm our result that selective maintenance is the mechanism that best explains differential spontaneous recovery.

To confirm this result, we required passing two tests: 1) The best model containing selective maintenance had to fit the data of the SR group better than the alternative models that did not contain selective maintenance specified in the pre-registration as per signed-rank tests for non-nested models and likelihood ratio tests for nested models; 2) The effect of selective maintenance on retention of latent cause counts, measured as (1-γ)•ω+γ , had to be significantly larger in the SR group as compared to the No SR group.
Before applying these tests, we performed the same model fitting procedure and group assignments as detailed above and in the pre-registered analysis plan.

As part of a baseline assessment, they then completed questionnaires (including the GAD7 as the only dimensional anxiety questionnaire) and a set of behavioral tasks (including the task described in this paper).
Subsequently, they engaged with a self-help tool for 5 weeks with additional symptom assessments throughout and after the time of the engagement.
Similar to Study 1 in the general population, participants were not included in the analyses if they failed questionnaire or behavioral attention checks or attempted the task twice.
We also excluded participants who were invited to participate in a brief zoom identity check but did not sign up or failed the identity check.
To avoid participants reporting symptoms untruthfully only in order to qualify for the study, participants were told that symptoms were not required to participate in the study.
However, during the screening process, we oversampled participants who had a PHQ9 score larger than 4, such that the majority of participants ( 95%) had at least mild symptoms of depression.

For each analysis, we first examined the distribution of the variables to determine whether a log transformation was indicated and whether to use linear regression or rank regression (and, where relevant, confirmed the choice of linear regression by analyzing the distributions of residuals).
When multiple anxiety scales were available, we employed multiple regression; otherwise, we used single regressions (or corresponding correlation analyses).
In situations where non-normality or skewness were present, linear regression was performed on tied-rank-transformed outcome and predictor variables.
Regression coefficients, R² , and adjusted R² , were estimated from the ranktransformed data.

Uncertainty in the coefficients and model fit was assessed using 10,000 subject-level bootstrap samples, with participants sampled with replacement and the rank transformation repeated within each sample.
Two-sided 95% bootstrap confidence intervals were calculated for regression coefficients, R² , and adjusted R² .
The significance of the overall model was assessed using 10,000 permutations of the ranked outcome while keeping the predictors fixed.

1 Supplementary method 1.1 Task and auditory setup for online study
We took a set of measures to ensure that remote participants listened to the aversive screams throughout the task and experienced them as unpleasant but not intolerable.
Prior to acquisition, participants were instructed to put on headphones.
They had to correctly complete an audio test where they heard a word and had to indicate what the word was, and the side (left or right) in which they heard it.
The goal of the latter question was to ensure use of headphones.
Next, to ensure the scream was not too loud, participants listened to a softly spoken audio clip and were instructed to turn down their volume if they could hear the speech clearly.
The clip was calibrated to be quiet, so that if the participant could just barely hear it, the subsequent aversive screams would be loud enough to be effective, but not unbearably loud.
This was followed by 6 practice trials with a different CS (a circle) and an emotionally-neutral sound.

Finally, participants were presented with an audio clip of one of the aversive screams and were instructed that they could adjust the volume one last time to ensure that the sound was unpleasant, but not intolerable.
To ensure that participants did not lower the volume during the task, six auditory attention checks were embedded throughout.
During each of these checks, participants saw a fixation cross on the screen and simultaneously heard a soft-spoken verbal instruction (e.g., "Press the letter F now.").
The speech was intentionally quiet; designed to be inaudible if the participant had turned the volume down too far.
While the fixation cross remained on screen, participants were expected to press the specified key in response.
If no correct response was given, the task automatically continued after 10 seconds.
At the start of the second part of the study (the spontaneous recovery test phase) participants returned from a break during which they completed a different task.
Before beginning the test phase, they were asked to rate their expectation of hearing a scream in response to each image.
Following this, they were presented with the scream audio clip once more and instructed to readjust the volume, if necessary, so that it was unpleasant but not intolerable.

We advertised the study on ResearchMatch, social media platforms (Instagram, Facebook, X, Reddit and TikTok), the newspaper (USA Today), and Cint.
Interested individuals could visit the study information page on our lab website, where they could find a link to the screening survey.

Participants were eligible to participate only if they met all the following criteria: • older than 18 years old • physically located in the US • fluent in English • no hearing problems • had access to a headphone • did not previously participate in studies from our lab • no one from the same household had participated in the study • not be receiving psychotherapy or plan to begin one within the next eight weeks • not be taking antidepressants, have changed the doses or type of antidepressants in the past four weeks, or plan to make such changes in the next eight weeks • their primary mental health concern was to improve their mood, reduce negative thoughts, enjoy more activities again, or reduce symptoms of depression.

Participants who met all the criteria and missed at most one of attention checks in the self-report questionnaires and the Raven's matrices test were immediately contacted by email with a link to the main study.
We oversampled participants who had a PHQ9 greater than 4 to ensure we could measure an improvement in depression scores at the end of the study (not part of the present analyses).
Thus, only approximately 5% of participants did not meet that criterion.
The main study lasted six weeks, consisting of three task batches, three questionnaire batches, and the use of a self-help tool for 5 weeks.
Participants had seven days to complete each of the batches.
Importantly, in the analyses reported here, we only included data from the baseline assessment, i.e., before participants engaged with the self-help tool.
Participants were asked to estimate the likelihood of various real-world events on a scale from 0% (never) to 100% (always).
The questions were as follows: • "How likely is it that the sun will rise tomorrow?"
• "How likely is it that a meteorite will hit Earth in the next month?"
• "Susan is having a baby.
How likely is it that the baby will be a girl?"
• "How likely is it to rain in the desert?"
• "How likely is the bus to be late during bad weather?"
In a separate section, participants were asked to judge how other people should respond to specific stimuli they observed.
Each scenario involved a fictional person seeing a colored circle on a screen ten times, followed by varying outcomes.
Participants were asked to indicate, on a scale from 0% (never) through 50% (half the time) to 100% (always), how likely they thought the stimulus would be followed by a scream.
The prompt read "Please indicate the response you think the person should give."
The scenarios were as follows: • Emma saw a green circle 10 times.
Each time, it was followed by a scream.
"How likely do you think the green circle will be followed by a scream?"
• Liam saw an orange circle 10 times.
It was never followed by a scream.
"How likely do you think the orange circle will be followed by a scream?"
• Noah saw a red circle 10 times.
It was followed by a scream on 5 random occasions and not followed by a scream on the other 5.
"How likely do you think the red circle will be followed by a scream?"
• Olivia saw a yellow circle 10 times.
It was followed by a scream the first 3 times but not the following 7 times.
"How likely do you think the yellow circle will be followed by a scream?"
These questions were designed to evaluate the responses styles and sensitivity of the participants when using a probability slider (0% -100%) to express the likelihood judgments.

For example, to check whether participants interpreted and used the slider appropriately and to observe whether they had a tendency to respond deterministically (e.g., 0% or 100%) or probabilistically (e.g., 50%) when evaluating uncertainty.
In our preregistration, we reported that our exploration dataset contained 378 data files and that we had included 318 in our analyses.
However, we later discovered that two subjects had been included twice.
We removed the duplicate files, which did not alter the pattern of our results.
We also noted a discrepancy in the replication dataset.
In our preregistration, we assumed that data from 377 participants were available for the replication analyses.
Upon accessing the data, we found that data from 60 additional subjects were availablepreviously uncounted due to a syncing error.
One subject was excluded from both datasets, because their file from the acquisition data, but not the spontaneous recovery data, was added to the exploratory dataset.
In our preregistration and original code, we had specified that we would use Wilcoxon signed-rank test to compare non-nested models and likelihood ratio tests to compare nested models.
Results using these tests are available in our first preprint version (https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/2kdtf v1).

text.text: However, in response to a suggestion from a reviewer, to accurately account for between-subject variability as well as non-normal and skewed distributions and outliers, we have updated our model comparison approach during revision and now examine whether the distribution of differences of AIC values between models differs from 0 using bootstrapping.
Our original and updated approaches, as well as bootstrapping of BIC differences, all identify models with selective maintenance as the winning models in line with our preregistered hypotheses.
