In study 2, 417 participants 2.3 Alternative frameworks, models and mechanisms
The most known and commonly applied model to explain conditioning phenomena is Rescorla and Wagner (1972).
text.formatted: The most known and commonly applied model to explain conditioning phenomena is <ref type="bibr">Rescorla and Wagner (1972)</ref>.

text.text: The Rescorla-Wagner model can be seen as a special case of the temporal difference algorithm in reinforcement learning without taking future outcomes into account.
(Note that in our design, each trial involves at most one outcome so this is an accurate simplification.)

According to the Rescorla-Wagner model, one learns the strength of the association between the CS and the US according to is the strength of the association between CS j and the US at the start of trial t (the value of the state defined by the CS j in reinforcement learning), η is the learning rate and r(t) is the outcome (US, in which case r(t) = 1 or no US, hence r(t) = 0) on trial t.
This model tracks average or expected US.
We fit such a model (as well as such a model with two learning rates, one for reinforced and one for non-reinforced trials) to our data.
It captured the relearning phase well, and the main features of the acquisition and extinction phase.
However, it (predictably) failed to capture spontaneous recovery.
The reason that this standard model is incapable of capturing spontaneous recovery is that reinforced and non-reinforced observations of the CS+ both update the same V CS+ .
Thus, these two types of events cannot be dissociated or have separate effects at a later time point.
Put simply, no memory of aversive events or states can come back as this information is not stored anywhere separately.
We also tested a somewhat related model with a decay rule (Erev & Roth, 1998), which tracks cumulative outcomes according to V j (t + 1) = V j (t) * γ + r(t).
text.formatted: We also tested a somewhat related model with a decay rule <ref type="bibr">(Erev & Roth, 1998)</ref>, which tracks cumulative outcomes according to V j (t + 1) = V j (t) * γ + r(t).

text.text: A model with the decay learning rule (and especially a version of it that additionally scaled r(t) by the salience parameter C) captured acquisition and extinction very well, but completely failed to capture spontaneous recovery and relearning.

Similar to the above delta rule model, the decay rule model fails to capture spontaneous recovery because it does not contain a mechanisms that stores information about aversive and non-aversive events separately.
In both models the 'states' that one learns about are predefined, here by the two CSs.
The extension that the latent cause framework offers is that allows to infer which states (called latent causes, or causes for shorthand) a participant learns about.
For example, some participants might infer that the moon and the candles belong to the same state, as they have the same color and a similar purpose, e.g., providing light in the dark.
We observed these participants in our dataset and termed them the Generalizers.
Other participants might infer one state per CS (as is assumed for all participants by standard reinforcement learning models).
Their behavior would be similar to the No SR group (and is well predicted by the Rescorla-Wagner model).

Note, however, that behavior of participants in the SR (which was the largest group in our sample comprising over half of the participants) was best explained by models inferring three states, one for the CS-, one for the CS+ in non-reinforced trials (that is, without a US) and one for the CS+ and the US.
This indicates that it is important to not predefine the number of states participants can learn about but assess how many states they likely inferred and learned about.
The prevailing theory explaining spontaneous recovery suggests that individuals infer different contexts during acquisition and extinction.
During a spontaneous recovery test-or simply at a later time in life-it may be unclear which context is currently active.

This ambiguity can lead to a prediction of aversive outcomes based on an average of the acquisition and extinction phases, or alternatively, the acquisition context may be retrieved, for instance, due to a visual cue indicating that an individual currently is in the acquisition context.
In the former case, one would expect a modest level of spontaneous recovery, while in the latter, a more substantial amount of spontaneous recovery would be observed.
To ensure that context cues cannot account for spontaneous recovery in our dataset, we designed our experiment to tightly control for context cues.
We ensured that no visual or auditory stimuli differentiated the task phases, making it unlikely that contextual inference could explain the observed spontaneous recovery.
However, we still observed substantial amounts of spontaneous recovery.
How could spontaneous recovery be explained through context inference in the absence of any context cues?
Bouton (1993 Bouton ( , 2004) ) proposed that temporal context may still play a role.
text.formatted: <ref type="bibr">Bouton (1993</ref> <ref type="bibr">Bouton ( , 2004) )</ref> proposed that temporal context may still play a role.

text.text: Similar to visual cues, other contextual elements -such as bodily states, room temperature, or ambient lighting -might support the inference of different temporal contexts, even if these variables were not explicitly manipulated or assessed.

As reviewed by DuBrow, Rouhani, Niv, and Norman (2017), neural evidence further suggests that we encode mental context that slowly drifts over time, possibly to bind events that occur in close temporal proximity together in memory. DuBrow et al. (2017) also proposed that mental context can shift abruptly due to surprising events (or boundaries) such that different mental contexts can be encoded separately to reduce interference in memory.
text.formatted: As reviewed by DuBrow, <ref type="bibr">Rouhani, Niv, and Norman (2017)</ref>, neural evidence further suggests that we encode mental context that slowly drifts over time, possibly to bind events that occur in close temporal proximity together in memory. <ref type="bibr">DuBrow et al. (2017)</ref> also proposed that mental context can shift abruptly due to surprising events (or boundaries) such that different mental contexts can be encoded separately to reduce interference in memory.

text.text: There are many ways to formalize the concept of temporal context, and we acknowledge that it is impossible to rule out every possible implementation.
Nevertheless, we attempted to formalize temporal context inference by implementing a hierarchical inference model.
This model not only infers latent causes but also allows for the inference of distinct temporal contexts (see Pisupati, Berwian, Chiu, Ren, & Niv, 2023).
text.formatted: This model not only infers latent causes but also allows for the inference of distinct temporal contexts (see <ref type="bibr">Pisupati, Berwian, Chiu, Ren, & Niv, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In this model, temporal contexts can contain several latent causes.

However, the occurrence of dissimilar or previously unseen combinations of latent causes can prompt the inference of a new temporal context-akin to how new latent causes are inferred from dissimilar observations (and in line with shifts in mental context).
We incorporated persistence into the model to formalize the assumption that contexts tend to remain stable over time.
This also incorporates the idea that "invisible" cues like lighting, temperature, or bodily states change slowly and are more stable within a task phase than across phases.
For a mathematical formalization of the model, see Pisupati et al. (2023).
text.formatted: For a mathematical formalization of the model, see <ref type="bibr">Pisupati et al. (2023)</ref>.

text.text: We fit this hierarchical temporal context model, along with reduced variants of itself and a version that included a salience parameter C (increasing counts of reinforced events as in the Salience Model), to data from our exploratory dataset (Study 1).
None of the models were able to simulate the amount of spontaneous recovery observed in our data given constraints of the overall data (such as unbiased priors over observations).
Furthermore, none of the models captured the average magnitude of spontaneous recovery when fit to the data or provided better fits across the complete task.

The main reason why these and related models failed to capture spontaneous recovery is because they can, on average, only predict spontaneous recovery up to the average of probability given all observations or the weighted average of the acquisition and extinction context, which in our task is p(US|CS+) = .235 at the beginning of the spontaneous recovery test.
Indeed, this is exactly what the Temporal Weighting Model (see Fig. 7 in the main paper) and other models predicted.
text.formatted: Indeed, this is exactly what the Temporal Weighting Model (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">7</ref> in the main paper) and other models predicted.

text.text: However, in our empirical data , the prediction of a US given the CS+ clearly exceeded .235 (see Fig. 2 and 7 and in the main text).
text.formatted: However, in our empirical data , the prediction of a US given the CS+ clearly exceeded .235 (see Fig. <ref type="figure">2</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">7</ref> and in the main text).

text.text: These results suggest that, at least in the form tested here, temporal contexts do not provide a sufficient explanation for the amount of spontaneous recovery observed in our data.
Importantly, we do not claim that temporal contexts do not exist.
Rather, without any additional mechanisms at play, they appear to be neither sufficient nor necessary to account for the behavioral effects observed during the spontaneous recovery test.
Early experiments measuring spontaneous recovery were often conducted in animals.
Fear responses were usually measured in terms of freezing (or flight) responses.
Such responses are more effortful than no response.
Hence, one plausible explanation brought forward for this behavior was response fatigue, which became more prevalent during extinction (see (Rescorla, 2004) for a review).
text.formatted: Hence, one plausible explanation brought forward for this behavior was response fatigue, which became more prevalent during extinction (see <ref type="bibr">(Rescorla, 2004)</ref> for a review).

text.text: Thus, no true extinction takes place: the lack of fear responses only appears as a result of response fatigue.
However, once that fatigue has passed, fear responses re-occur, which could look like the return of fear with time, i.e., spontaneous recovery.

However, response fatigue is not able to account for spontaneous recovery in our paradigm as responses of aversive outcome predictions or negative affect on the rating scales required the same amount of effort for all responses (i.e., independent of its valence or probability of a negative outcome).

In an attempt to reduce the probability that we missed alternative explanations for spontaneous recovery, we also tested models with additional free parameters (such as a free b obs which allows for biased starting priors), different priors over observations for features (CSs) and outcomes (US), additional combinations of free parameters such as the temporal weighting and salience or selective maintenance, and longer time intervals (e.g., double the number of break stimuli) in the Temporal Weighting, the Decay and the Salience Model.

Furthermore, we tested a model that included no decay but rather strengthening of latent causes that predict the US (i.e., the "excitatory association" in theories of extinction), and a model that included only decay of latent causes that do not predict the US (i.e., the "inhibitory association" in theories of extinction).
All these models either did not capture spontaneous recovery together with the entire dataset well or did not capture it to the same extent as models with selective maintenance.

We also tested alternative implementations of the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model, e.g., independent decay parameters for aversive and non-aversive latent causes and a model that only allowed selective maintenance during the break, or an additional free parameter that influenced the extent to which selective maintenance was applied during task phases in addition to the break.
However, the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model was the best constraint and identifiable model given our dataset.

Our goal was to find the best model that explains spontaneous recovery given the entire data without biasing our results to one specific model with our modeling choices while achieving parameter and model identifiability.
Below, we briefly explain why we made a set of modeling choices and how we verified that they did not bias our results.
We fixed the concentration parameter α to 0.03 for all models except the Basic Concentration Model.
This decision was based on the fact that both α and the prior over observations a obs influence the number of latent causes that are generated, leading to potential parameter identifiability issues.

Since the Basic Prior Model fit the data better than the Basic Concentration Model (see Fig. 5 in the main text), and a obs offers a more direct psychological interpretation, we opted to fix α rather than fit both parameters simultaneously, especially as doing so did not capture any additional meaningful patterns in the behavioral data.
text.formatted: Since the Basic Prior Model fit the data better than the Basic Concentration Model (see Fig. <ref type="figure">5</ref> in the main text), and a obs offers a more direct psychological interpretation, we opted to fix α rather than fit both parameters simultaneously, especially as doing so did not capture any additional meaningful patterns in the behavioral data.

text.text: The value of α = 0.03 was chosen based on simulations conducted before collecting the exploratory dataset.
These simulations showed that this fixed value could reproduce the full range of behavioral patterns observed in pilot data.

Model fits on the exploratory dataset further confirmed that setting α above zero but keeping it rather small yielded consistent qualitative results, though it could shift other parameter estimates in a uniform way.

The Selective Maintenance Model without a free salience parameter provided a better fit to the data than all alternative and reduced models, and reproduced the same pattern of results as the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model.
This suggests that including a salience parameter is not necessary to mechanistically explain the data or the phenomenon of spontaneous recovery.
However, at the individual level, the Selective Maintenance Model failed to capture spontaneous recovery in approximately 40% of participants in the spontaneous recovery (SR) group.

Comparing participants whose data were well fit by the Selective Maintenance Model to those whose data were not revealed a key difference: in the latter group, there was no evidence of selective maintenance during the task phases.
One possibility that can explain their behavior is that these participants might use selective maintenance only during the break, resembling an 'offline' learning effect.
To differentiate between 'online' and 'offline' learning, we tested a model that included both selective maintenance and a free (unconstrained) salience parameter.

While this model again reproduced the same overall pattern of results, it introduced a parameter identifiability issue in some participants, particularly those showing strong selective maintenance or salience effects during learning.
This is because both parameters can influence behavior in similar ways during the learning phase.
However, only selective maintenance can exert an effect during the break.
To address this issue, we constrained the salience parameter to C low ≤ 1, limiting its influence and improving identifiability.
Importantly, applying or removing this constraint did not affect the overall pattern of results or their interpretation in either the selective maintenance or decay models.
To ensure that our winning model was not selected simply because it can flexibly fit data generated by fundamentally different processes, we conducted a model recovery analysis.

This analysis included only models based on processes that were distinct from each other (that is, we did not include nested models, as they are by design confusable given the setting of the nested parameters): the Basic Concentration Model, the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model, the Processing Loss Model, and the Temporal Weighting Model.
We first generated synthetic data using each model and the best-fitting parameter estimates obtained from participants in the SR group.
(Note that we focused on the SR group, because our main research question focused on identifying the mechanisms that explain spontaneous recovery.)
We added response noise to the simulated US predictions according to the empirically estimated standard deviation σ and truncated values below 0 or above 1 to 0 and 1, respectively.
Next, we fit all four models to the data generated by each model in turn.
For each simulated dataset, we identified the model that best explained the data based on the lowest BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) value.
We then recorded the proportion of simulated 'participants' for whom each model was recovered as best-fitting.
As shown in Suppl.
Fig. 3, the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model (second row and column) was reliably recovered and was almost never selected as the best-fitting model for data it did not generate.
text.formatted: Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">3</ref>, the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model (second row and column) was reliably recovered and was almost never selected as the best-fitting model for data it did not generate.

text.text: In contrast, the Processing Loss Model was frequently miss-identified as having been generated by the Temporal Weighting Model.
This suggests that at least our task design does not allow us to tease apart whether data were generated by the Processing Loss Model or the Temporal Weighting Model.

However, since neither of these two models were the winning model in any of our model comparison tests, and all models were compared statistically only to the models with selective maintenance (and not to each other), this finding does not affect our overall results and conclusions.

The fact that the two models are confusable notwithstanding, we can conclude from our results that the theory that spontaneous recovery occurs due to lack of novelty or neural fatigue in the extinction phase (e.g., Pavlov (1927)) cannot account for spontaneous recovery in our empirical data.

1 Supplementary method 1.1 Task and auditory setup for online study 1.1.1 Audio setup and checks
We took a set of measures to ensure that remote participants listened to the aversive screams throughout the task and experienced them as unpleasant but not intolerable.
Prior to acquisition, participants were instructed to put on headphones.
They had to correctly complete an audio test where they heard a word and had to indicate what the word was, and the side (left or right) in which they heard it.
The goal of the latter question was to ensure use of headphones.
Next, to ensure the scream was not too loud, participants listened to a softly spoken audio clip and were instructed to turn down their volume if they could hear the speech clearly.
The clip was calibrated to be quiet, so that if the participant could just barely hear it, the subsequent aversive screams would be loud enough to be effective, but not unbearably loud.
This was followed by 6 practice trials with a different CS (a circle) and an emotionally-neutral sound.

Finally, participants were presented with an audio clip of one of the aversive screams and were instructed that they could adjust the volume one last time to ensure that the sound was unpleasant, but not intolerable.
To ensure that participants did not lower the volume during the task, six auditory attention checks were embedded throughout.
During each of these checks, participants saw a fixation cross on the screen and simultaneously heard a soft-spoken verbal instruction (e.g., "Press the letter F now.").
The speech was intentionally quiet; designed to be inaudible if the participant had turned the volume down too far.
While the fixation cross remained on screen, participants were expected to press the specified key in response.
If no correct response was given, the task automatically continued after 10 seconds.
At the start of the second part of the study (the spontaneous recovery test phase) participants returned from a break during which they completed a different task.
Before beginning the test phase, they were asked to rate their expectation of hearing a scream in response to each image.
Following this, they were presented with the scream audio clip once more and instructed to readjust the volume, if necessary, so that it was unpleasant 1 but not intolerable.

The most known and commonly applied model to explain conditioning phenomena is Rescorla and Wagner (1972).
text.formatted: The most known and commonly applied model to explain conditioning phenomena is <ref type="bibr">Rescorla and Wagner (1972)</ref>.

text.text: The Rescorla-Wagner model can be seen as a special case of the temporal difference algorithm in reinforcement learning without taking future outcomes into account.
(Note that in our design, each trial involves at most one outcome so this is an accurate simplification.)

According to the Rescorla-Wagner model, one learns the strength of the association between the CS and the US according is the strength of the association between CS j and the US at the start of trial t (the value of the state defined by the CS j in reinforcement learning), η is the learning rate and r(t) is the outcome (US, in which case r(t) = 1 or no US, hence r(t) = 0) on trial t.
This model tracks average or expected US.
We fit such a model (as well as such a model with two learning rates, one for reinforced and one for non-reinforced trials) to our data.
It captured the relearning phase well, and the main features of the acquisition and extinction phase.
However, it (predictably) failed to capture spontaneous recovery.
The reason that this standard model is incapable of capturing spontaneous recovery is that reinforced and non-reinforced observations of the CS+ both update the same V CS+ .
Thus, these two types of events cannot be dissociated or have separate effects at a later time point.
Put simply, no memory of aversive events or states can come back as this information is not stored anywhere separately.
We also tested a somewhat related model with a decay rule (Erev & Roth, 1998), which tracks cumulative outcomes according to V j (t + 1) = V j (t) * γ + r(t).
text.formatted: We also tested a somewhat related model with a decay rule <ref type="bibr">(Erev & Roth, 1998)</ref>, which tracks cumulative outcomes according to V j (t + 1) = V j (t) * γ + r(t).

text.text: A model with the decay learning rule (and especially a version of it that additionally scaled r(t) by the salience parameter C) captured acquisition and extinction very well, but completely failed to capture spontaneous recovery and relearning.

Similar to the above delta rule model, the decay rule model fails to capture spontaneous recovery because it does not contain a mechanisms that stores information about aversive and non-aversive events separately.
In both models the 'states' that one learns about are predefined, here by the two CSs.
The extension that the latent cause framework offers is that allows to infer which states (called latent causes, or causes for shorthand) a participant learns about.
For example, some participants might infer that the moon and the candles belong to the same state, as they have the same color and a similar purpose, e.g., providing light in the dark.
We observed these participants in our dataset and termed them the Generalizers.
Other participants might infer one state per CS (as is assumed for all participants by standard reinforcement learning models).
Their behavior would be similar to the No SR group (and is well predicted by the Rescorla-Wagner model).

Note, however, that behavior of participants in the SR (which was the largest group in our sample comprising over half of the participants) was best explained by models inferring three states, one for the CS-, one for the CS+ in non-reinforced trials (that is, without a US) and one for the CS+ and the US.
This indicates that it is important to not predefine the number of states participants can learn about but assess how many states they likely inferred and learned about.
The prevailing theory explaining spontaneous recovery suggests that individuals infer different contexts during acquisition and extinction.
During a spontaneous recovery test-or simply at a later time in life-it may be unclear which context is currently active.

This ambiguity can lead to a prediction of aversive outcomes based on an average of the acquisition and extinction phases, or alternatively, the acquisition context may be retrieved, for instance, due to a visual cue indicating that an individual currently is in the acquisition context.
In the former case, one would expect a modest level of spontaneous recovery, while in the latter, a more substantial amount of spontaneous recovery would be observed.
To ensure that context cues cannot account for spontaneous recovery in our dataset, we designed our experiment to tightly control for context cues.
We ensured that no visual or auditory stimuli differentiated the task phases, making it unlikely that contextual inference could explain the observed spontaneous recovery.
However, we still observed substantial amounts of spontaneous recovery.
How could spontaneous recovery be explained through context inference in the absence of any context cues?
Bouton (1993 Bouton ( , 2004) ) proposed that temporal context may still play a role.
text.formatted: <ref type="bibr">Bouton (1993</ref> <ref type="bibr">Bouton ( , 2004) )</ref> proposed that temporal context may still play a role.

text.text: Similar to visual cues, other contextual elements -such as bodily states, room temperature, or ambient lighting -might support the inference of different temporal contexts, even if these variables were not explicitly manipulated or assessed.

As reviewed by DuBrow, Rouhani, Niv, and Norman (2017), neural evidence further suggests that we encode mental context that slowly drifts over time, possibly to bind events that occur in close temporal proximity together in memory. DuBrow et al. (2017) also proposed that mental context can shift abruptly due to surprising events (or boundaries) such that different mental contexts can be encoded separately to reduce interference in memory.
text.formatted: As reviewed by DuBrow, <ref type="bibr">Rouhani, Niv, and Norman (2017)</ref>, neural evidence further suggests that we encode mental context that slowly drifts over time, possibly to bind events that occur in close temporal proximity together in memory. <ref type="bibr">DuBrow et al. (2017)</ref> also proposed that mental context can shift abruptly due to surprising events (or boundaries) such that different mental contexts can be encoded separately to reduce interference in memory.

text.text: There are many ways to formalize the concept of temporal context, and we acknowledge that it is impossible to rule out every possible implementation.
Nevertheless, we attempted to formalize temporal context inference by implementing a hierarchical inference model.
This model not only infers latent causes but also allows for the inference of distinct temporal contexts (see Pisupati, Berwian, Chiu, Ren, & Niv, 2023).
text.formatted: This model not only infers latent causes but also allows for the inference of distinct temporal contexts (see <ref type="bibr">Pisupati, Berwian, Chiu, Ren, & Niv, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In this model, temporal contexts can contain several latent causes.

However, the occurrence of dissimilar or previously unseen combinations of latent causes can prompt the inference of a new temporal context-akin to how new latent causes are inferred from dissimilar observations (and in line with shifts in mental context).
We incorporated persistence into the model to formalize the assumption that contexts tend to remain stable over time.
This also incorporates the idea that "invisible" cues like lighting, temperature, or bodily states change slowly and are more stable within a task phase than across phases.
For a mathematical formalization of the model, see Pisupati et al. (2023).
text.formatted: For a mathematical formalization of the model, see <ref type="bibr">Pisupati et al. (2023)</ref>.

text.text: We fit this hierarchical temporal context model, along with reduced variants of itself and a version that included a salience parameter C (increasing counts of reinforced events as in the Salience Model), to data from our exploratory dataset (Study 1).
None of the models were able to simulate the amount of spontaneous recovery observed in our data given constraints of the overall data (such as unbiased priors over observations).
Furthermore, none of the models captured the average magnitude of spontaneous recovery when fit to the data or provided better fits across the complete task.

The main reason why these and related models failed to capture spontaneous recovery is because they can, on average, only predict spontaneous recovery up to the average of probability given all observations or the weighted average of the acquisition and extinction context, which in our task is p(US|CS+) = .235 at the beginning of the spontaneous recovery test.
Indeed, this is exactly what the Temporal Weighting Model (see Fig. 7 in the main paper) and other models predicted.
text.formatted: Indeed, this is exactly what the Temporal Weighting Model (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">7</ref> in the main paper) and other models predicted.

text.text: However, in our empirical data , the prediction of a US given the CS+ clearly exceeded .235 (see Fig. 2 and 7 and in the main text).
text.formatted: However, in our empirical data , the prediction of a US given the CS+ clearly exceeded .235 (see Fig. <ref type="figure">2</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">7</ref> and in the main text).

text.text: These results suggest that, at least in the form tested here, temporal contexts do not provide a sufficient explanation for the amount of spontaneous recovery observed in our data.
Importantly, we do not claim that temporal contexts do not exist.
Rather, without any additional mechanisms at play, they appear to be neither sufficient nor necessary to account for the behavioral effects observed during the spontaneous recovery test.
Early experiments measuring spontaneous recovery were often conducted in animals.
Fear responses were usually measured in terms of freezing (or flight) responses.
Such responses are more effortful than no response.
Hence, one plausible explanation brought forward for this behavior was response fatigue, which became more prevalent during extinction (see (Rescorla, 2004) for a review).
text.formatted: Hence, one plausible explanation brought forward for this behavior was response fatigue, which became more prevalent during extinction (see <ref type="bibr">(Rescorla, 2004)</ref> for a review).

text.text: Thus, no true extinction takes place: the lack of fear responses only appears as a result of response fatigue.
However, once that fatigue has passed, fear responses re-occur, which could look like the return of fear with time, i.e., spontaneous recovery.

However, response fatigue is not able to account for spontaneous recovery in our paradigm as responses of aversive outcome predictions or negative affect on the rating scales required the same amount of effort for all responses (i.e., independent of its valence or probability of a negative outcome).

In an attempt to reduce the probability that we missed alternative explanations for spontaneous recovery, we also tested models with additional free parameters (such as a free b obs which allows for biased starting priors), different priors over observations for features (CSs) and outcomes (US), additional combinations of free parameters such as the temporal weighting and salience or selective maintenance, and longer time intervals (e.g., double the number of break stimuli) in the Temporal Weighting, the Decay and the Salience Model.

Furthermore, we tested a model that included no decay but rather strengthening of latent causes that predict the US (i.e., the "excitatory association" in theories of extinction), and a model that included only decay of latent causes that do not predict the US (i.e., the "inhibitory association" in theories of extinction).
All these models either did not capture spontaneous recovery together with the entire dataset well or did not capture it to the same extent as models with selective maintenance.

We also tested alternative implementations of the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model, e.g., independent decay parameters for aversive and non-aversive latent causes and a model that only allowed selective maintenance during the break, or an additional free parameter that influenced the extent to which selective maintenance was applied during task phases in addition to the break.
However, the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model was the best constraint and identifiable model given our dataset.

Our goal was to find the best model that explains spontaneous recovery given the entire data without biasing our results to one specific model with our modeling choices while achieving parameter and model identifiability.
Below, we briefly explain why we made a set of modeling choices and how we verified that they did not bias our results.
We fixed the concentration parameter α to 0.03 for all models except the Basic Concentration Model.
This decision was based on the fact that both α and the prior over observations a obs influence the number of latent causes that are generated, leading to potential parameter identifiability issues.

Since the Basic Prior Model fit the data better than the Basic Concentration Model (see Fig. 5 in the main text), and a obs offers a more direct psychological interpretation, we opted to fix α rather than fit both parameters simultaneously, especially as doing so did not capture any additional meaningful patterns in the behavioral data.
text.formatted: Since the Basic Prior Model fit the data better than the Basic Concentration Model (see Fig. <ref type="figure">5</ref> in the main text), and a obs offers a more direct psychological interpretation, we opted to fix α rather than fit both parameters simultaneously, especially as doing so did not capture any additional meaningful patterns in the behavioral data.

text.text: The value of α = 0.03 was chosen based on simulations conducted before collecting the exploratory dataset.
These simulations showed that this fixed value could reproduce the full range of behavioral patterns observed in pilot data.

Model fits on the exploratory dataset further confirmed that setting α above zero but keeping it rather small yielded consistent qualitative results, though it could shift other parameter estimates in a uniform way.

The Selective Maintenance Model without a free salience parameter provided a better fit to the data than all alternative and reduced models, and reproduced the same pattern of results as the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model.
This suggests that including a salience parameter is not necessary to mechanistically explain the data or the phenomenon of spontaneous recovery.
However, at the individual level, the Selective Maintenance Model failed to capture spontaneous recovery in approximately 40% of participants in the spontaneous recovery (SR) group.

Comparing participants whose data were well fit by the Selective Maintenance Model to those whose data were not revealed a key difference: in the latter group, there was no evidence of selective maintenance during the task phases.
One possibility that can explain their behavior is that these participants might use selective maintenance only during the break, resembling an 'offline' learning effect.

text.text: To differentiate between 'online' and 'offline' learning, we tested a model that included both selective maintenance and a free (unconstrained) salience parameter.

While this model again reproduced the same overall pattern of results, it introduced a parameter identifiability issue in some participants, particularly those showing strong selective maintenance or salience effects during learning.
This is because both parameters can influence behavior in similar ways during the learning phase.
However, only selective maintenance can exert an effect during the break.
To address this issue, we constrained the salience parameter to C low ≤ 1, limiting its influence and improving identifiability.
Importantly, applying or removing this constraint did not affect the overall pattern of results or their interpretation in either the selective maintenance or decay models.
To ensure that our winning model was not selected simply because it can flexibly fit data generated by fundamentally different processes, we conducted a model recovery analysis.

This analysis included only models based on processes that were distinct from each other (that is, we did not include nested models, as they are by design confusable given the setting of the nested parameters): the Basic Concentration Model, the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model, the Processing Loss Model, and the Temporal Weighting Model.
We first generated synthetic data using each model and the best-fitting parameter estimates obtained from participants in the SR group.
(Note that we focused on the SR group, because our main research question focused on identifying the mechanisms that explain spontaneous recovery.)
We added response noise to the simulated US predictions according to the empirically estimated standard deviation σ and truncated values below 0 or above 1 to 0 and 1, respectively.
Next, we fit all four models to the data generated by each model in turn.
For each simulated dataset, we identified the model that best explained the data based on the lowest BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) value.
We then recorded the proportion of simulated 'participants' for whom each model was recovered as best-fitting.
As shown in Suppl.
Fig. 3, the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model (second row and column) was reliably recovered and was almost never selected as the best-fitting model for data it did not generate.
text.formatted: Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_22">3</ref>, the Selective Maintenance and Low Salience Model (second row and column) was reliably recovered and was almost never selected as the best-fitting model for data it did not generate.

text.text: In contrast, the Processing Loss Model was frequently miss-identified as having been generated by the Temporal Weighting Model.
This suggests that at least our task design does not allow us to tease apart whether data were generated by the Processing Loss Model or the Temporal Weighting Model.

However, since neither of these two models were the winning model in any of our model comparison tests, and all models were compared statistically only to the models with selective maintenance (and not to each other), this finding does not affect our overall results and conclusions.

The fact that the two models are confusable notwithstanding, we can conclude from our results that the theory that spontaneous recovery occurs due to lack of novelty or neural fatigue in the extinction phase (e.g., Pavlov (1927)) cannot account for spontaneous recovery in our empirical data.

C) The effects of cognitive restructuring at the start of extinction (black arrow), which we implemented through a change in the priors for new latent causes, is to lead to more generalization between the two latent causes and thus decreasing the impact of selective maintenance.

D) Spaced extinction, implemented by spreading extinction trials throughout both the extinction and long break phases (black horizontal bar), protects the safe latent cause from decay and therefore decreases the relative strength of the dangerous latent cause and reduces spontaneous recovery.
E) Schema therapy, implemented as a reduction of the selective maintenance results in stronger decay of the dangerous latent cause.

F) Retrieval cues used after the end of extinction (therapy) decrease the decay of the safe latent cause, therefore leaving the relative strength of the safe and dangerous latent causes flat throughout the break, and preventing spontaneous recovery.
